The same receipt's control mode kept 3 members and ended with 4 including C (observed at parsed index 5; that comparison was scored unknown because both modes shared a result event name, which the dedicated control experiment has now replaced with a scored holds).; a8b8d696ac934beda1434a93b5d7758f-gap-1: model declares resolved: Resolved affirmatively by retained receipts 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c, 11dea1fdcb6d4f089a373fe6c1d3a36e, 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903 and 108a83830e904d90a9236738033c2c74: the silently created two-server change {A,B,C} -> {A,B,E} commits on the stale leader A plus the promoted, caught-up nonvoter E while the old voter B is partitioned (witness index 2 in each execution: change_err nil, committed true, the configuration entry present on A and on E, B still one index short); the old majority {B,C} then elects B in a higher term while A still leads its own configuration with E's acknowledgements (witness index 3 or 6: old_leader B in term 4 with a_still_leader true); and after the partition heals A's committed entry is replaced by the new leader's entry (witness index 7, committed_entry_truncated true), leaving the two sides with different logs and different applied state (fsm_a_logs 6 against fsm_b_logs 5). The direct route the earlier answer identified as impossible stays impossible - a voter that never receives the entry is strictly behind and is refused by voters that hold it (raft.go 1731-1746, 1812-1828) - which is exactly why the construction needs the entry to commit without one old voter, made possible by the promoted nonvoter and by the new configuration entering the commitment on append (raft.go 1236-1241).; 1ed9540f22fe4fa9bef3b3bda88e22e8-gap-2: model declares resolved: Resolved by retained receipt 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c (scored): the silent two-server change {A,B,C} -> {A,B,E} committed on A plus the promoted caught-up nonvoter E (parsed index 2: change_err nil, x_index 11, committed=true, entry type LogConfiguration on A and on E, A commit index 11, B still at log index 10); the old majority {B,C} elected B in term 4 while A was still leader in term 3 (parsed index 3, comparison violated with witness 3), i.e. two concurrent leaders with disjoint support over the same log; and after healing, A's entry at index 11 became a LogNoop of term 4 (parsed index 4, comparison violated with witness 4), so the entry committed under the configuration recorded in the logs was truncated on the node that had committed it. The earlier receipt 79d93a5aaad448888cc04214be8f2ad8 reproduced the same observations but its comparisons were unscored because of my identity wiring; it is retained as the superseded revision of the same harness.

Historical interpretation `60a1ad6dc8744f1d9c027eb86bcbe3e7-interpretation-0` · declared predicate does not hold; model defect claim: defect asserted (subject to independent verification): Summary of the current account for this question: the trigger is RestoreCommittedLogs=true with a CommitTrackingLogStore, a log whose newest configuration entry is at or below the persisted commit index, and no snapshot whose ConfigurationIndex covers that entry. Under that trigger the restarted node reconstructs its configuration only from the snapshot, so three consequence classes follow, each with retained control-backed receipts, plus a client-contract consequence recorded further below: (a) a missing membership context - empty configuration when there is no snapshot, which stops all campaigns and leaves a live quorum unable to elect (receipts 430d7ba602ed4666bdfe63a96c71e2fc, 4f4a771f03b649c2a5703b0ff279ff3a, 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837); (b) decisions taken from a stale base - a single AddVoter becomes the two-server change {A,B,C}->{A,B,E}, which silently drops a voter, and with a partitioned old voter produces concurrent leaders over the same log, truncation of the entry the stale leader had committed and divergent FSM state (receipts d2d1cb0951b74a2984ec525710e4c740, 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c, 11dea1fdcb6d4f089a373fe6c1d3a36e and e5ad9e5149fa4255b61e7826bf6b8064); (c) stale membership accounting - a resurrected removed voter or a forgotten added voter makes the leader accept writes that the configuration committed in the log has not acknowledged (receipts 226f9762f0b444f69c154b35fe0788f3 with 7adf927d528b4a74942c03b155aa8557, and b1daa1f4c9444b8d857bc7e0ab761691 with ec2c61af79bd42d7a5fe00657b7aeb22). Boundary: a snapshot covering the newest configuration entry, or leaving the flag at its default, removes every one of these observations in the controls, and once the stale configuration is adopted nothing re-reads the log for configurations, so it persists until one of three events repairs it: a snapshot is installed (the configuration comes from the snapshot metadata), a later configuration entry reaches the node through appendEntries and is processed by processConfigurationLogEntry (raft.go 1569-1578, which installs the full membership the leader computed), or the node is restarted without the flag. In the empty-configuration cases the first two repairs need a leader, which is exactly what the empty configuration prevents. A repeat of the simultaneous-restart experiment reproduced the same failure and control values, so the headline progress claim also rests on two scored executions. Three independent receipts, all retained. (1) 430d7ba602ed4666bdfe63a96c71e2fc index 1: with RestoreCommittedLogs=true and no snapshot the restarting node returns with an empty configuration (servers_after=0 against servers_before=1), never campaigns again in a 3s opportunity, and logs 'no known peers, aborting election'; both the non-replay run (index 3) and the snapshot run (index 5) keep the configuration and re-elect. (2) d2d1cb0951b74a2984ec525710e4c740 index 1: with a snapshot carrying {A,B}@1 and a committed AddVoter C at index 8 with staged commit 11, the restarted node reports 2 servers while its continuously running peer reports 3 and its own log still holds the newest configuration entry; index 3: a later AddVoter E then returns no error and both nodes converge on 3 members without C (contains_c_final=false), i.e. a legitimately added voter is silently removed from the cluster by a change computed from the stale base. (3) edfd3c204c654542a8bdb4263f290d4d index 1: the isolated control with RestoreCommittedLogs=false scores holds (servers_after=1 against the same bootstrapped voter), so the replayed committed prefix, not restart itself, is the cause. (4) 4f4a771f03b649c2a5703b0ff279ff3a index 1: restarting all three voters at once with the flag leaves servers_after=[0,0,0] and nodes_with_full_config=0 with no leader in a six-second opportunity, while the same procedure without the flag scores holds at index 3 (nodes_with_full_config=3, leader elected) - a cluster-wide progress loss, not a single node's lost context. (5) 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837: with only two of three voters restarted, the untouched configured voter leads with the configuration-less nodes' votes (index 0, servers_after=[0,0,3]); once that voter stops, the two remaining live, fully up-to-date voters cannot elect a leader in six seconds at 50ms timeouts (index 1, log last index 13 on both), while the control without the flag re-elects immediately (index 3). Source chain: restoreFromCommittedLogs raises lastApplied to the persisted commit index (api.go 723-755); the configuration scan then begins at max(lastSnapshot,lastApplied)+1 (api.go 611-613), so configuration entries inside the committed prefix are never fed to their only producer processConfigurationLogEntry (raft.go 1605-1623) unless a snapshot carries them (api.go 645-689). With Servers empty the follower refuses to campaign (raft.go 230-234 on every heartbeat timeout, raft.go 214-251) and both vote handlers skip their membership checks (raft.go 1663-1672, 1780-1784); with Servers stale, appendConfigurationEntry derives the next membership from that stale base (raft.go 1204-1241, configuration.go 224-302) once the admission gate sees latest==committed (raft.go 654-664). (6) 79d93a5aaad448888cc04214be8f2ad8: with A's configuration coming from a snapshot ({A,B}) while its log holds the newer {A,B,C} entry, AddVoter E returned no error and the silently created two-server change committed at index 11 with A's commit index at 11 and E holding the same LogConfiguration entry (parsed index 2), while B stayed at log index 10 with the old membership; the old majority {B,C} then elected B in term 4 while A was still leader in term 3 (parsed index 3, a_still_leader=true), and after the partition healed A's entry 11 was a LogNoop of term 4 rather than the committed configuration entry (parsed index 4, committed_entry_truncated=true). Receipt 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c from the corrected harness scored both comparisons: entry at index 11 truncated after heal (violated, witness index 4) and a_still_leader=true while the old side elected B in term 4 (violated, witness index 3), with the silent change itself at index 2 (change_err nil, committed=true, LogConfiguration on A and E, B at log index 10). The repeat receipt 11dea1fdcb6d4f089a373fe6c1d3a36e reproduced the same outcome under schedule variation (setup catch-up indices differed: C ended at log index 8 instead of 9): silent change committed at index 11 with entry type LogConfiguration on A and E (index 2), B elected in term 4 while A still led in term 3 (index 3, comparison violated), and the entry truncated after healing (index 4, comparison violated). Receipt e5ad9e5149fa4255b61e7826bf6b8064 (extended harness) scores both comparisons violated with witness index 5: the entry at the created index is truncated after healing, and after a client command returned success and was acknowledged and committed on the {A,B,E} leader (parsed index 3: write_applied=true, applied_a=12, fsm_a_logs=6) the FSM contents differ afterwards (fsm_a_logs=6 versus fsm_b_logs=5), so the client-visible effect survives only on the node whose log lost the entry.  A fourth consequence direction belongs to the client contracts: on the same stale leader, VerifyLeader confirms leadership from the stale quorum while a different majority of the committed configuration elects a leader in a higher term (receipt 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903, witness index 6), so the read-safety protection clients rely on is not effective in that state. Why the competing-majority outcome is attributable to the stale base rather than to the partition: with a correct configuration the same partition geometry cannot commit the change at all, because the change installs its own membership into the commitment and that membership still contains the partitioned voter, so its quorum cannot be reached (a single-server change from {A,B,C} needs two of three including the partitioned member's replacement geometry, and in the four-voter case the new quorum is three of four). The stale base both shrinks the base the change is computed from and replaces a voter, which is why the new member set's quorum can be met by A plus one other node while the partitioned voter stays out - and that is precisely what the D2 receipts show, with the control mode refusing the same write under the committed membership. Mechanism locators for the two steps that turn the stale base into those outcomes: the new configuration is installed into the leader's commitment as soon as the change entry is appended (raft.go 1236-1241), which is what lets the silently created member set be acknowledged by the stale leader plus one other node, and appendEntries clears a conflicting log suffix when terms differ (raft.go 1522-1553), which is what removes the entry the stale leader had committed once the higher-term leader reaches it; the vote freshness checks that keep the removed voter itself from winning are at raft.go 1731-1746 and 1812-1828.

Interpretation counterevidence: The isolated control receipt edfd3c204c654542a8bdb4263f290d4d scores holds with the identical restart and no snapshot (servers_after=1), so the loss is caused by replaying the committed prefix, not by restart, snapshot absence, or the commit-tracking store.; The snapshot run inside the first receipt (index 5) keeps the configuration, so the defect requires the newest configuration entry to be inside the skipped prefix; a snapshot taken after the change masks it.; Voter C never runs in the two-voter probe, so nothing in the receipts shows C resisting or noticing its removal; the claim is about the configuration the running nodes decide with.; The cluster-wide receipt 4f4a771f03b649c2a5703b0ff279ff3a scores the control comparison holds (index 3, nodes_with_full_config=3) and the failing case violated (index 1, nodes_with_full_config=0), so the empty configuration after a simultaneous restart is specific to the replayed committed prefix.; Receipt 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837 scores the control comparison holds (index 3: the two live voters re-elect a leader without the flag) and the failing case violated (index 1: after the configured voter stops, no leader among the two live voters although both hold every committed entry, log last index 13 on both), so the loss of electability is tied to the missing configuration rather than to the restart or the shutdown.; The dual-majority path needs a caught-up nonvoter E so the silent change can commit without the partitioned voter B; without such a node the change would need B's acknowledgement and B would then hold the new membership.; Two independent executions of the corrected dual-majority experiment (receipts 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c and 11dea1fdcb6d4f089a373fe6c1d3a36e) produced the same entry index, the same concurrent leadership and the same truncation, so the outcome is reproducible rather than a single-run timing artifact.; In that extended execution the stale leader had already stepped down when the old side's leader was sampled (index 4, a_still_leader=false), which is why leader concurrency is reported as an observed window from the two earlier executions rather than as a comparison in the current harness.; Repeat receipt c1dcda29549b48c7a775adfc2e9a4bda reproduced the simultaneous-restart outcome exactly (servers_after [0,0,0], nodes_with_full_config 0, no leader in the observation window; control [3,3,3] with a leader elected at index 3), so the cluster-wide progress loss is reproducible under schedule variation (the staged commit indices differed from the first run: [11 10 11] against [11 11 9]).; Repeat receipt e0ef28c2bc89481aa6b3af478422de7c reproduced all three modes of the original probe with the same values: with RestoreCommittedLogs and no snapshot the node returns with an empty configuration and does not lead again (index 1), while the non-replay mode keeps its configuration and leads (index 3) and the snapshot mode keeps its configuration and leads (index 5).; Repeat receipt 2963a0b01d97404dbf946e7b87a214f8 reproduced the partial-restart outcome exactly (two restarted voters with empty configurations, the untouched voter leading at index 2 with nodes_with_full=1, then no leader among the two live voters holding log index 13 apiece; control re-electing at index 0), so the live-quorum progress loss is reproducible as well.; The revised dual-majority execution (receipt 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903) scored all three comparisons as predicted: the committed entry is truncated after healing (violated, witness 7), the FSMs diverge after an acknowledged write (violated, witness 7, fsm_a_logs 6 against fsm_b_logs 5), and the stale leader confirmed leadership while the old majority led in a higher term (violated, witness 6: verify_ok true, old_leader B in term 4, a_still_leader true).; The repeat of the client-contract revision (receipt 108a83830e904d90a9236738033c2c74) reproduced all three comparison outcomes (truncation violated at witness 7, FSM divergence violated at witness 7, confirmation-while-another-leader violated at witness 6 with verify_ok true, old_leader B in term 4 and A still leading), so that consequence is reproducible.; The repair execution also acts as counterevidence against reading the stale configuration as irrecoverable: a later configuration entry from a correctly configured leader restored the forgotten voter on the restarted node (receipt 6d6abaf163524e64878c6c9810de2461, comparison and witness index 5).; Boundary control: with the same operations but without the commits that push the persisted commit index past the removal entry, the restarted node keeps the committed membership and the removed voter stays removed (receipt 457abd18451d4fd18ed506ae7f5c5391, comparison and witness index 9), so the loss is tied to the entry lying inside the replayed prefix and not to the restart or the removal itself.; The boundary control repeated: receipt 4fe974e4e3cc491984791b8a812c5886 reproduced every comparison of the boundary revision (resurrection violated at index 1, premature commit violated at index 3, flag-off control holding at index 7, and the shallow case holding at index 9 with two servers and the removed voter absent), so the trigger boundary is reproducible and not a schedule artifact.; Counterevidence that limits the impact of the cluster-wide loss rather than the finding: the same stores, restarted once more with the flag disabled, came back fully configured and elected a leader (receipt 81163da076c64417bd48e0f79260d73d, comparison and witness index 2), so the state is operator-recoverable without touching durable data.; Causal refinement, observed rather than argued: the same stores and the same flag produced a good outcome while nothing had been staged and the failure once the flag-on path had staged a commit index (receipt 656e33fb90f24c58a94928eeeeb938aa, comparison holds at index 1 and violated at index 3), so the deciding condition is the persisted commit index named in the trigger, not merely enabling the feature.; Causal refinement reproduced: repeat receipt 202311f4911e4af5828d49134f37811c produced the identical values and outcomes (staged zero with the configuration kept through the first flagged restart, holds at index 1; staged nine afterwards and the configuration lost on the next one, violated at witness index 3), so the contrast that pins the trigger to the persisted commit index is stable across executions.
Interpretation limitations: All executions are in-process in-memory clusters at protocol version 3 with 50ms heartbeat/election timeouts and a single committed configuration change; joint-consensus or multi-step changes are not exercised.; The finding is specific to RestoreCommittedLogs=true with a CommitTrackingLogStore; with the flag disabled the same durable state recovers normally in every receipt.; The configuration-less nodes still act as voters in other respects (they granted the configured voter's election win in receipt 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837, index 0), which is why the cluster survived until that voter stopped; this is read from the receipt and from the membership checks being skipped for an empty configuration (raft.go 1663-1672, 1780-1784).; In that probe the partitioned side elects its leader with 3s election timeouts (reloaded to keep the restarted leader from losing the first election), so the interval is seconds; the ordering it demonstrates does not depend on those particular values.; The dual-majority probe has no control variant: with the flag disabled the leader's configuration is current, so the same AddVoter is a single-server change and cannot create disjoint majorities (nextConfiguration over the current configuration, configuration.go 224-302).; Leader concurrency on the two sides was observed with A still leading in four executions (receipts 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c, 11dea1fdcb6d4f089a373fe6c1d3a36e, 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903 and 108a83830e904d90a9236738033c2c74) while one revision of the harness observed A already stepped down when the old side's leader was sampled, so the window is real but its length is schedule-dependent; the reproducible consequences are the truncation of the committed entry and the resulting FSM divergence.; The child question is now established by retained receipt 226f9762f0b444f69c154b35fe0788f3 (resurrected membership and a write applied on the leader with B, required by the committed configuration, never receiving the entry; control refuses the same write), so the parents' consequence list includes premature commitment under a stale membership.; Two consequences reached by later receipts are no longer pending: the cluster-wide and partial-restart progress losses (receipts 4f4a771f03b649c2a5703b0ff279ff3a and 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837) and the premature-commit-under-a-stale-membership consequence (receipt 226f9762f0b444f69c154b35fe0788f3 with its repeat 7adf927d528b4a74942c03b155aa8557).; A source check of which snapshot the library considers newest found the expected protection: SnapshotStore implementations rank candidates by term then index (file_snapshot.go 535-547 with List at 286), so the newest snapshot is selected; no evidence of a snapshot-selection defect was found, and none is claimed.; The third consequence direction is now established by retained receipt b1daa1f4c9444b8d857bc7e0ab761691: a restarted leader that forgets an added voter accepted a write held by only two of the four committed voters, while the control refused it.; A check of the captured documentation found no statement about this feature outside the source: RestoreCommittedLogs and CommitTrackingLogStore appear only in config.go, log.go and api.go, and never in README.md, docs/README.md, docs/apply.md, docs/divergence.md, membership.md or CHANGELOG.md (those files do mention snapshots elsewhere, so the search itself is sound). The only normative text is the Config field comment, which requires the commit-tracking store but nothing about snapshots or configuration recovery, so no documented caller duty defeats the premise.; In the original probe and its repeat the two control modes share the comparison event names with the failing mode, so their comparisons are scored unknown; the scored control for the non-replay restart comes from the separate isolated-control experiment (receipt edfd3c204c654542a8bdb4263f290d4d, holds).; Correction of the repair-path statement: an earlier version of the summary said only a snapshot install or an operator restart repairs a stale configuration. A later configuration entry does too, because appendEntries processes new configuration entries and installs the membership encoded in them (raft.go 1569-1578); the three repair paths are now stated explicitly. This correction does not change any comparison or receipt; it narrows the persistence claim.; The client-contract consequence is now established by retained receipt 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903: VerifyLeader returned success on the stale-membership leader (its own acknowledgement plus the promoted voter's) in the same execution in which the old majority elected B in term 4 while that leader still considered itself leader, so the documented protection against returning stale data does not hold in this state.; The repair path is now executed as well: receipt 6d6abaf163524e64878c6c9810de2461 (index 5) shows the stale node restored to five members including the forgotten voter D and the newly added E once a correctly configured leader replicated a later configuration entry to it, with the other four comparisons in that execution unchanged (membership violated at index 1, premature commit violated at index 3, controls holding at indices 7 and 9). Boundary that follows: repair needs a correctly configured leader, so it is available where the stale nodes are a minority (the forgotten-voter case) and unavailable where the empty configuration prevents any leader from being elected (the cluster-wide and partial-restart cases).; Process note kept for traceability: receipt 8f0b76d0cd49441c81ecb603f1fcd527 is a build failure of the superseded revision of the partial-restart harness (helpers declared in a sibling file that is not copied for execution); my repeat request had named that superseded experiment instead of its correction b826595f01b844f9b95efe7b29d757dd-experiment. The receipt carries no evidence and is deliberately absent from this interpretation's executions map because a build failure yields no parsed observations; the cited partial-restart observations come only from the corrected revision.; The trigger boundary is now executed in both directions by receipt 457abd18451d4fd18ed506ae7f5c5391: in the shallow case the staged commit index is 5 while the removal entry sits at index 6, so the scan covers it and the restarted node keeps the committed membership (comparison holds at index 9: two servers, removed voter absent, one peer, and the partitioned write refused), whereas the same harness with two extra commits has the removal entry at index 7 with staged commit 7 and resurrects the removed voter (violated at index 1) and accepts the write (violated at index 3; control holds at index 7). The condition 'configuration entry at or below the persisted commit index' in the trigger summary is therefore execution-confirmed rather than reasoned.; Boundary of the empty-configuration case, kept explicit because it limits the consequence: what is lost is membership context and the ability to campaign, not data flow. In the partial-restart receipts (7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837 and its repeat 2963a0b01d97404dbf946e7b87a214f8) the two configuration-less nodes still appended and applied entries up to log index 13 while the correctly configured voter led, and they still granted the votes that let it win, so replication through a configured leader continues; the observable harm is their empty self-view (no campaigns, no peers) and, once the configured voter stops, the cluster-wide loss of electability recorded in those same receipts.; Citation audit: every receipt index cited by the current interpretations was re-read from the retained observations and matches the claim it supports (empty configuration and no leadership at 430d7ba602ed4666bdfe63a96c71e2fc index 1 and its repeat e0ef28c2bc89481aa6b3af478422de7c index 1; all three voters empty at 4f4a771f03b649c2a5703b0ff279ff3a index 1 and c1dcda29549b48c7a775adfc2e9a4bda index 1; no leader among the two live voters at 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837 index 1 and 2963a0b01d97404dbf946e7b87a214f8 index 1; silent change, concurrent leader and truncation at 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c indices 2, 3, 4; leader confirmation, confirmation-while-another-leader and truncation plus FSM divergence at 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903 indices 4, 6, 7 and confirmation-while-another-leader again at 108a83830e904d90a9236738033c2c74 index 6; stale membership and the dropped voter at d2d1cb0951b74a2984ec525710e4c740 indices 1 and 3; applied client write and FSM divergence at e5ad9e5149fa4255b61e7826bf6b8064 indices 3 and 5; resurrection and premature commit at 226f9762f0b444f69c154b35fe0788f3 indices 1 and 3 and their repeat 7adf927d528b4a74942c03b155aa8557 indices 1 and 3; forgotten voter and understated quorum at b1daa1f4c9444b8d857bc7e0ab761691 indices 1 and 3 and repeat ec2c61af79bd42d7a5fe00657b7aeb22 indices 1 and 3; repair at 6d6abaf163524e64878c6c9810de2461 index 5; boundary at 457abd18451d4fd18ed506ae7f5c5391 indices 1 and 9 and its repeat 4fe974e4e3cc491984791b8a812c5886 indices 1 and 9).; Reachability boundary on the snapshot repair path: although an installed snapshot does carry the configuration (raft.go 1953-1961), a leader sends a snapshot only when the follower lacks entries the leader has already compacted, and a node whose configuration was lost this way has a complete log (the loss comes from skipping entries, not from missing them), so no snapshot is ever sent to it in these scenarios. The snapshot path therefore repairs new or behind nodes, while a stale-but-complete node is repaired only by an operator restart without the flag or by a later configuration entry from a correctly configured leader, as executed.; Operator recovery is now executed (receipt 0440f054115e44f4a0234c7a4ef67150): in the empty-configuration state live bootstrap refuses with 'bootstrap only works on new clusters' and leaves the node empty (violated, index 1), while RecoverCluster on the stopped node restores the supplied configuration and the node leads again within three seconds (holds, index 2). The repair picture is therefore complete and operational: a later configuration entry from a correctly configured leader, a restart with the flag disabled, or RecoverCluster on a stopped node; not live bootstrap, and not an incoming snapshot for a node whose log is already complete.; The operator remediation for the cluster-wide case is now executed (receipt 81163da076c64417bd48e0f79260d73d): the flagged simultaneous restart left every voter empty with no leader (violated, index 1, staged commit indices [11 11 11]), and stopping the same three nodes and restarting them on the same stores with the flag disabled restored the configuration on all three and produced a leader (holds at index 2, nodes_with_full_config 3, leader index 1; control unchanged at index 4). The consequence of the headline progress loss is therefore bounded: it is in-memory and reversible by an ordinary restart, with no durable state discarded and no configuration change needed, but nothing in-protocol can repair it while it lasts.; Precision on what the truncation removes, taken from the same receipts rather than reasoned: in both executions that carry the client write (e5ad9e5149fa4255b61e7826bf6b8064 index 5 and 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903 index 7) the stale leader's log end falls from index 12 to 11 after healing while its applied index stays at 12 and its FSM still holds six commands against the new leader's five. The entry removed is therefore not only the configuration change at index 11 but also the client command the leader had committed and applied at index 12, and the two sides' applied state differs by exactly that command. This is the client-visible form of the safety violation: an acknowledged write is deleted from the log of the node that acknowledged it, while the divergent FSM keeps its effect.; The causal refinement is executed (receipt 656e33fb90f24c58a94928eeeeb938aa): the cluster that had only run with the flag disabled carried a staged commit index of 0 and kept its configuration through the first flagged restart (comparison holds, index 1), then staged 9 through its own writes while the flag was on (index 2) and lost the configuration on the next flagged restart (violated, witness index 3, zero servers and no leader). The trigger is therefore the persisted commit index relative to the newest configuration entry, not the flag by itself, and the first restart after enabling the feature can look harmless.; The latent-trap experiment has been executed twice with identical values (receipts 656e33fb90f24c58a94928eeeeb938aa and 202311f4911e4af5828d49134f37811c), so the causal refinement rests on a reproduced contrast rather than a single run.

The same receipt's control mode kept 3 members and ended with 4 including C (observed at parsed index 5; that comparison was scored unknown because both modes shared a result event name, which the dedicated control experiment has now replaced with a scored holds).; a8b8d696ac934beda1434a93b5d7758f-gap-1: model declares resolved: Resolved affirmatively by retained receipts 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c, 11dea1fdcb6d4f089a373fe6c1d3a36e, 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903 and 108a83830e904d90a9236738033c2c74: the silently created two-server change {A,B,C} -> {A,B,E} commits on the stale leader A plus the promoted, caught-up nonvoter E while the old voter B is partitioned (witness index 2 in each execution: change_err nil, committed true, the configuration entry present on A and on E, B still one index short); the old majority {B,C} then elects B in a higher term while A still leads its own configuration with E's acknowledgements (witness index 3 or 6: old_leader B in term 4 with a_still_leader true); and after the partition heals A's committed entry is replaced by the new leader's entry (witness index 7, committed_entry_truncated true), leaving the two sides with different logs and different applied state (fsm_a_logs 6 against fsm_b_logs 5). The direct route the earlier answer identified as impossible stays impossible - a voter that never receives the entry is strictly behind and is refused by voters that hold it (raft.go 1731-1746, 1812-1828) - which is exactly why the construction needs the entry to commit without one old voter, made possible by the promoted nonvoter and by the new configuration entering the commitment on append (raft.go 1236-1241).; 1ed9540f22fe4fa9bef3b3bda88e22e8-gap-2: model declares resolved: Resolved by retained receipt 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c (scored): the silent two-server change {A,B,C} -> {A,B,E} committed on A plus the promoted caught-up nonvoter E (parsed index 2: change_err nil, x_index 11, committed=true, entry type LogConfiguration on A and on E, A commit index 11, B still at log index 10); the old majority {B,C} elected B in term 4 while A was still leader in term 3 (parsed index 3, comparison violated with witness 3), i.e. two concurrent leaders with disjoint support over the same log; and after healing, A's entry at index 11 became a LogNoop of term 4 (parsed index 4, comparison violated with witness 4), so the entry committed under the configuration recorded in the logs was truncated on the node that had committed it. The earlier receipt 79d93a5aaad448888cc04214be8f2ad8 reproduced the same observations but its comparisons were unscored because of my identity wiring; it is retained as the superseded revision of the same harness.

Historical interpretation `bcd5cdc4fd144dedb0f418cf0424a490-interpretation-0` · declared predicate does not hold; model defect claim: defect asserted (subject to independent verification): Summary of the current account for this question: the trigger is RestoreCommittedLogs=true with a CommitTrackingLogStore, a log whose newest configuration entry is at or below the persisted commit index, and no snapshot whose ConfigurationIndex covers that entry. Under that trigger the restarted node reconstructs its configuration only from the snapshot, so three consequence classes follow, each with retained control-backed receipts, plus a client-contract consequence recorded further below: (a) a missing membership context - empty configuration when there is no snapshot, which stops all campaigns and leaves a live quorum unable to elect (receipts 430d7ba602ed4666bdfe63a96c71e2fc, 4f4a771f03b649c2a5703b0ff279ff3a, 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837); (b) decisions taken from a stale base - a single AddVoter becomes the two-server change {A,B,C}->{A,B,E}, which silently drops a voter, and with a partitioned old voter produces concurrent leaders over the same log, truncation of the entry the stale leader had committed and divergent FSM state (receipts d2d1cb0951b74a2984ec525710e4c740, 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c, 11dea1fdcb6d4f089a373fe6c1d3a36e and e5ad9e5149fa4255b61e7826bf6b8064); (c) stale membership accounting - a resurrected removed voter or a forgotten added voter makes the leader accept writes that the configuration committed in the log has not acknowledged (receipts 226f9762f0b444f69c154b35fe0788f3 with 7adf927d528b4a74942c03b155aa8557, and b1daa1f4c9444b8d857bc7e0ab761691 with ec2c61af79bd42d7a5fe00657b7aeb22). Boundary: a snapshot covering the newest configuration entry, or leaving the flag at its default, removes every one of these observations in the controls, and once the stale configuration is adopted nothing re-reads the log for configurations, so it persists until one of three events repairs it: a snapshot is installed (the configuration comes from the snapshot metadata), a later configuration entry reaches the node through appendEntries and is processed by processConfigurationLogEntry (raft.go 1569-1578, which installs the full membership the leader computed), or the node is restarted without the flag. In the empty-configuration cases the first two repairs need a leader, which is exactly what the empty configuration prevents. A repeat of the simultaneous-restart experiment reproduced the same failure and control values, so the headline progress claim also rests on two scored executions. Three independent receipts, all retained. (1) 430d7ba602ed4666bdfe63a96c71e2fc index 1: with RestoreCommittedLogs=true and no snapshot the restarting node returns with an empty configuration (servers_after=0 against servers_before=1), never campaigns again in a 3s opportunity, and logs 'no known peers, aborting election'; both the non-replay run (index 3) and the snapshot run (index 5) keep the configuration and re-elect. (2) d2d1cb0951b74a2984ec525710e4c740 index 1: with a snapshot carrying {A,B}@1 and a committed AddVoter C at index 8 with staged commit 11, the restarted node reports 2 servers while its continuously running peer reports 3 and its own log still holds the newest configuration entry; index 3: a later AddVoter E then returns no error and both nodes converge on 3 members without C (contains_c_final=false), i.e. a legitimately added voter is silently removed from the cluster by a change computed from the stale base. (3) edfd3c204c654542a8bdb4263f290d4d index 1: the isolated control with RestoreCommittedLogs=false scores holds (servers_after=1 against the same bootstrapped voter), so the replayed committed prefix, not restart itself, is the cause. (4) 4f4a771f03b649c2a5703b0ff279ff3a index 1: restarting all three voters at once with the flag leaves servers_after=[0,0,0] and nodes_with_full_config=0 with no leader in a six-second opportunity, while the same procedure without the flag scores holds at index 3 (nodes_with_full_config=3, leader elected) - a cluster-wide progress loss, not a single node's lost context. (5) 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837: with only two of three voters restarted, the untouched configured voter leads with the configuration-less nodes' votes (index 0, servers_after=[0,0,3]); once that voter stops, the two remaining live, fully up-to-date voters cannot elect a leader in six seconds at 50ms timeouts (index 1, log last index 13 on both), while the control without the flag re-elects immediately (index 3). Source chain: restoreFromCommittedLogs raises lastApplied to the persisted commit index (api.go 723-755); the configuration scan then begins at max(lastSnapshot,lastApplied)+1 (api.go 611-613), so configuration entries inside the committed prefix are never fed to their only producer processConfigurationLogEntry (raft.go 1605-1623) unless a snapshot carries them (api.go 645-689). With Servers empty the follower refuses to campaign (raft.go 230-234 on every heartbeat timeout, raft.go 214-251) and both vote handlers skip their membership checks (raft.go 1663-1672, 1780-1784); with Servers stale, appendConfigurationEntry derives the next membership from that stale base (raft.go 1204-1241, configuration.go 224-302) once the admission gate sees latest==committed (raft.go 654-664). (6) 79d93a5aaad448888cc04214be8f2ad8: with A's configuration coming from a snapshot ({A,B}) while its log holds the newer {A,B,C} entry, AddVoter E returned no error and the silently created two-server change committed at index 11 with A's commit index at 11 and E holding the same LogConfiguration entry (parsed index 2), while B stayed at log index 10 with the old membership; the old majority {B,C} then elected B in term 4 while A was still leader in term 3 (parsed index 3, a_still_leader=true), and after the partition healed A's entry 11 was a LogNoop of term 4 rather than the committed configuration entry (parsed index 4, committed_entry_truncated=true). Receipt 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c from the corrected harness scored both comparisons: entry at index 11 truncated after heal (violated, witness index 4) and a_still_leader=true while the old side elected B in term 4 (violated, witness index 3), with the silent change itself at index 2 (change_err nil, committed=true, LogConfiguration on A and E, B at log index 10). The repeat receipt 11dea1fdcb6d4f089a373fe6c1d3a36e reproduced the same outcome under schedule variation (setup catch-up indices differed: C ended at log index 8 instead of 9): silent change committed at index 11 with entry type LogConfiguration on A and E (index 2), B elected in term 4 while A still led in term 3 (index 3, comparison violated), and the entry truncated after healing (index 4, comparison violated). Receipt e5ad9e5149fa4255b61e7826bf6b8064 (extended harness) scores both comparisons violated with witness index 5: the entry at the created index is truncated after healing, and after a client command returned success and was acknowledged and committed on the {A,B,E} leader (parsed index 3: write_applied=true, applied_a=12, fsm_a_logs=6) the FSM contents differ afterwards (fsm_a_logs=6 versus fsm_b_logs=5), so the client-visible effect survives only on the node whose log lost the entry.  A fourth consequence direction belongs to the client contracts: on the same stale leader, VerifyLeader confirms leadership from the stale quorum while a different majority of the committed configuration elects a leader in a higher term (receipt 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903, witness index 6), so the read-safety protection clients rely on is not effective in that state. Why the competing-majority outcome is attributable to the stale base rather than to the partition: with a correct configuration the same partition geometry cannot commit the change at all, because the change installs its own membership into the commitment and that membership still contains the partitioned voter, so its quorum cannot be reached (a single-server change from {A,B,C} needs two of three including the partitioned member's replacement geometry, and in the four-voter case the new quorum is three of four). The stale base both shrinks the base the change is computed from and replaces a voter, which is why the new member set's quorum can be met by A plus one other node while the partitioned voter stays out - and that is precisely what the D2 receipts show, with the control mode refusing the same write under the committed membership. Mechanism locators for the two steps that turn the stale base into those outcomes: the new configuration is installed into the leader's commitment as soon as the change entry is appended (raft.go 1236-1241), which is what lets the silently created member set be acknowledged by the stale leader plus one other node, and appendEntries clears a conflicting log suffix when terms differ (raft.go 1522-1553), which is what removes the entry the stale leader had committed once the higher-term leader reaches it; the vote freshness checks that keep the removed voter itself from winning are at raft.go 1731-1746 and 1812-1828.

Voter C never runs in the two-voter probe, so nothing in the receipts shows C resisting or noticing its removal; the claim is about the configuration the running nodes decide with.; The cluster-wide receipt 4f4a771f03b649c2a5703b0ff279ff3a scores the control comparison holds (index 3, nodes_with_full_config=3) and the failing case violated (index 1, nodes_with_full_config=0), so the empty configuration after a simultaneous restart is specific to the replayed committed prefix.; boundary at 457abd18451d4fd18ed506ae7f5c5391 indices 1 and 9 and its repeat 4fe974e4e3cc491984791b8a812c5886 indices 1 and 9).; Reachability boundary on the snapshot repair path: although an installed snapshot does carry the configuration (raft.go 1953-1961), a leader sends a snapshot only when the follower lacks entries the leader has already compacted, and a node whose configuration was lost this way has a complete log (the loss comes from skipping entries, not from missing them), so no snapshot is sent to it in these scenarios (with the caveat, found while re-reading the snapshot path, that a leader-side user restore leaves a hole above such a node's next index and does send it one, replication.go 222-224 with raft.go 1097-1199). The snapshot path therefore repairs new or behind nodes, while a stale-but-complete node is repaired only by an operator restart without the flag or by a later configuration entry from a correctly configured leader, as executed.; Operator recovery is now executed (receipt 0440f054115e44f4a0234c7a4ef67150): in the empty-configuration state live bootstrap refuses with 'bootstrap only works on new clusters' and leaves the node empty (violated, index 1), while RecoverCluster on the stopped node restores the supplied configuration and the node leads again within three seconds (holds, index 2). The repair picture is therefore complete and operational: a later configuration entry from a correctly configured leader, a restart with the flag disabled, or RecoverCluster on a stopped node; not live bootstrap, and not an incoming snapshot for a node whose log is already complete.; The operator remediation for the cluster-wide case is now executed (receipt 81163da076c64417bd48e0f79260d73d): the flagged simultaneous restart left every voter empty with no leader (violated, index 1, staged commit indices [11 11 11]), and stopping the same three nodes and restarting them on the same stores with the flag disabled restored the configuration on all three and produced a leader (holds at index 2, nodes_with_full_config 3, leader index 1; control unchanged at index 4). The consequence of the headline progress loss is therefore bounded: it is in-memory and reversible by an ordinary restart, with no durable state discarded and no configuration change needed, but nothing in-protocol can repair it while it lasts.; Precision on what the truncation removes, taken from the same receipts rather than reasoned: in both executions that carry the client write (e5ad9e5149fa4255b61e7826bf6b8064 index 5 and 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903 index 7) the stale leader's log end falls from index 12 to 11 after healing while its applied index stays at 12 and its FSM still holds six commands against the new leader's five. The entry removed is therefore not only the configuration change at index 11 but also the client command the leader had committed and applied at index 12, and the two sides' applied state differs by exactly that command. This is the client-visible form of the safety violation: an acknowledged write is deleted from the log of the node that acknowledged it, while the divergent FSM keeps its effect.; The causal refinement is executed (receipt 656e33fb90f24c58a94928eeeeb938aa): the cluster that had only run with the flag disabled carried a staged commit index of 0 and kept its configuration through the first flagged restart (comparison holds, index 1), then staged 9 through its own writes while the flag was on (index 2) and lost the configuration on the next flagged restart (violated, witness index 3, zero servers and no leader). The trigger is therefore the persisted commit index relative to the newest configuration entry, not the flag by itself, and the first restart after enabling the feature can look harmless.; The latent-trap experiment has been executed twice with identical values (receipts 656e33fb90f24c58a94928eeeeb938aa and 202311f4911e4af5828d49134f37811c), so the causal refinement rests on a reproduced contrast rather than a single run.

Historical interpretation `c6ab2e18e9c34a7ea9e06a93ea6a048d-interpretation-0` · declared predicate does not hold; model defect claim: defect asserted (subject to independent verification): Summary of the current account for this question: the trigger is RestoreCommittedLogs=true with a CommitTrackingLogStore, a log whose newest configuration entry is at or below the persisted commit index, and no snapshot whose ConfigurationIndex covers that entry. Under that trigger the restarted node reconstructs its configuration only from the snapshot, so three consequence classes follow, each with retained control-backed receipts, plus a client-contract consequence recorded further below: (a) a missing membership context - empty configuration when there is no snapshot, which stops all campaigns and leaves a live quorum unable to elect (receipts 430d7ba602ed4666bdfe63a96c71e2fc, 4f4a771f03b649c2a5703b0ff279ff3a, 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837); (b) decisions taken from a stale base - a single AddVoter becomes the two-server change {A,B,C}->{A,B,E}, which silently drops a voter, and with a partitioned old voter produces concurrent leaders over the same log, truncation of the entry the stale leader had committed and divergent FSM state (receipts d2d1cb0951b74a2984ec525710e4c740, 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c, 11dea1fdcb6d4f089a373fe6c1d3a36e and e5ad9e5149fa4255b61e7826bf6b8064); (c) stale membership accounting - a resurrected removed voter or a forgotten added voter makes the leader accept writes that the configuration committed in the log has not acknowledged (receipts 226f9762f0b444f69c154b35fe0788f3 with 7adf927d528b4a74942c03b155aa8557, and b1daa1f4c9444b8d857bc7e0ab761691 with ec2c61af79bd42d7a5fe00657b7aeb22). Boundary: a snapshot covering the newest configuration entry, or leaving the flag at its default, removes every one of these observations in the controls, and once the stale configuration is adopted nothing re-reads the log for configurations, so it persists until one of three events repairs it: a snapshot is installed (the configuration comes from the snapshot metadata), a later configuration entry reaches the node through appendEntries and is processed by processConfigurationLogEntry (raft.go 1569-1578, which installs the full membership the leader computed), or the node is restarted without the flag. In the empty-configuration cases the first two repairs need a leader, which is exactly what the empty configuration prevents. A repeat of the simultaneous-restart experiment reproduced the same failure and control values, so the headline progress claim also rests on two scored executions. Three independent receipts, all retained. (1) 430d7ba602ed4666bdfe63a96c71e2fc index 1: with RestoreCommittedLogs=true and no snapshot the restarting node returns with an empty configuration (servers_after=0 against servers_before=1), never campaigns again in a 3s opportunity, and logs 'no known peers, aborting election'; both the non-replay run (index 3) and the snapshot run (index 5) keep the configuration and re-elect. (2) d2d1cb0951b74a2984ec525710e4c740 index 1: with a snapshot carrying {A,B}@1 and a committed AddVoter C at index 8 with staged commit 11, the restarted node reports 2 servers while its continuously running peer reports 3 and its own log still holds the newest configuration entry; index 3: a later AddVoter E then returns no error and both nodes converge on 3 members without C (contains_c_final=false), i.e. a legitimately added voter is silently removed from the cluster by a change computed from the stale base. (3) edfd3c204c654542a8bdb4263f290d4d index 1: the isolated control with RestoreCommittedLogs=false scores holds (servers_after=1 against the same bootstrapped voter), so the replayed committed prefix, not restart itself, is the cause. (4) 4f4a771f03b649c2a5703b0ff279ff3a index 1: restarting all three voters at once with the flag leaves servers_after=[0,0,0] and nodes_with_full_config=0 with no leader in a six-second opportunity, while the same procedure without the flag scores holds at index 3 (nodes_with_full_config=3, leader elected) - a cluster-wide progress loss, not a single node's lost context. (5) 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837: with only two of three voters restarted, the untouched configured voter leads with the configuration-less nodes' votes (index 0, servers_after=[0,0,3]); once that voter stops, the two remaining live, fully up-to-date voters cannot elect a leader in six seconds at 50ms timeouts (index 1, log last index 13 on both), while the control without the flag re-elects immediately (index 3). Source chain: restoreFromCommittedLogs raises lastApplied to the persisted commit index (api.go 723-755); the configuration scan then begins at max(lastSnapshot,lastApplied)+1 (api.go 611-613), so configuration entries inside the committed prefix are never fed to their only producer processConfigurationLogEntry (raft.go 1605-1623) unless a snapshot carries them (api.go 645-689). With Servers empty the follower refuses to campaign (raft.go 230-234 on every heartbeat timeout, raft.go 214-251) and both vote handlers skip their membership checks (raft.go 1663-1672, 1780-1784); with Servers stale, appendConfigurationEntry derives the next membership from that stale base (raft.go 1204-1241, configuration.go 224-302) once the admission gate sees latest==committed (raft.go 654-664). (6) 79d93a5aaad448888cc04214be8f2ad8: with A's configuration coming from a snapshot ({A,B}) while its log holds the newer {A,B,C} entry, AddVoter E returned no error and the silently created two-server change committed at index 11 with A's commit index at 11 and E holding the same LogConfiguration entry (parsed index 2), while B stayed at log index 10 with the old membership; the old majority {B,C} then elected B in term 4 while A was still leader in term 3 (parsed index 3, a_still_leader=true), and after the partition healed A's entry 11 was a LogNoop of term 4 rather than the committed configuration entry (parsed index 4, committed_entry_truncated=true). Receipt 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c from the corrected harness scored both comparisons: entry at index 11 truncated after heal (violated, witness index 4) and a_still_leader=true while the old side elected B in term 4 (violated, witness index 3), with the silent change itself at index 2 (change_err nil, committed=true, LogConfiguration on A and E, B at log index 10). The repeat receipt 11dea1fdcb6d4f089a373fe6c1d3a36e reproduced the same outcome under schedule variation (setup catch-up indices differed: C ended at log index 8 instead of 9): silent change committed at index 11 with entry type LogConfiguration on A and E (index 2), B elected in term 4 while A still led in term 3 (index 3, comparison violated), and the entry truncated after healing (index 4, comparison violated). Receipt e5ad9e5149fa4255b61e7826bf6b8064 (extended harness) scores both comparisons violated with witness index 5: the entry at the created index is truncated after healing, and after a client command returned success and was acknowledged and committed on the {A,B,E} leader (parsed index 3: write_applied=true, applied_a=12, fsm_a_logs=6) the FSM contents differ afterwards (fsm_a_logs=6 versus fsm_b_logs=5), so the client-visible effect survives only on the node whose log lost the entry.  A fourth consequence direction belongs to the client contracts: on the same stale leader, VerifyLeader confirms leadership from the stale quorum while a different majority of the committed configuration elects a leader in a higher term (receipt 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903, witness index 6), so the read-safety protection clients rely on is not effective in that state. Why the competing-majority outcome is attributable to the stale base rather than to the partition: with a correct configuration the same partition geometry cannot commit the change at all, because the change installs its own membership into the commitment and that membership still contains the partitioned voter, so its quorum cannot be reached (a single-server change from {A,B,C} needs two of three including the partitioned member's replacement geometry, and in the four-voter case the new quorum is three of four). The stale base both shrinks the base the change is computed from and replaces a voter, which is why the new member set's quorum can be met by A plus one other node while the partitioned voter stays out - and that is precisely what the D2 receipts show, with the control mode refusing the same write under the committed membership. Mechanism locators for the two steps that turn the stale base into those outcomes: the new configuration is installed into the leader's commitment as soon as the change entry is appended (raft.go 1236-1241), which is what lets the silently created member set be acknowledged by the stale leader plus one other node, and appendEntries clears a conflicting log suffix when terms differ (raft.go 1522-1553), which is what removes the entry the stale leader had committed once the higher-term leader reaches it; the vote freshness checks that keep the removed voter itself from winning are at raft.go 1731-1746 and 1812-1828.

Interpretation counterevidence: The isolated control receipt edfd3c204c654542a8bdb4263f290d4d scores holds with the identical restart and no snapshot (servers_after=1), so the loss is caused by replaying the committed prefix, not by restart, snapshot absence, or the commit-tracking store.; The snapshot run inside the first receipt (index 5) keeps the configuration, so the defect requires the newest configuration entry to be inside the skipped prefix; a snapshot taken after the change masks it.; Voter C never runs in the two-voter probe, so nothing in the receipts shows C resisting or noticing its removal; the claim is about the configuration the running nodes decide with.; The cluster-wide receipt 4f4a771f03b649c2a5703b0ff279ff3a scores the control comparison holds (index 3, nodes_with_full_config=3) and the failing case violated (index 1, nodes_with_full_config=0), so the empty configuration after a simultaneous restart is specific to the replayed committed prefix.; Receipt 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837 scores the control comparison holds (index 3: the two live voters re-elect a leader without the flag) and the failing case violated (index 1: after the configured voter stops, no leader among the two live voters although both hold every committed entry, log last index 13 on both), so the loss of electability is tied to the missing configuration rather than to the restart or the shutdown.; The dual-majority path needs a caught-up nonvoter E so the silent change can commit without the partitioned voter B; without such a node the change would need B's acknowledgement and B would then hold the new membership.; Two independent executions of the corrected dual-majority experiment (receipts 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c and 11dea1fdcb6d4f089a373fe6c1d3a36e) produced the same entry index, the same concurrent leadership and the same truncation, so the outcome is reproducible rather than a single-run timing artifact.; In that extended execution the stale leader had already stepped down when the old side's leader was sampled (index 4, a_still_leader=false), which is why leader concurrency is reported as an observed window from the two earlier executions rather than as a comparison in the current harness.; Repeat receipt c1dcda29549b48c7a775adfc2e9a4bda reproduced the simultaneous-restart outcome exactly (servers_after [0,0,0], nodes_with_full_config 0, no leader in the observation window; control [3,3,3] with a leader elected at index 3), so the cluster-wide progress loss is reproducible under schedule variation (the staged commit indices differed from the first run: [11 10 11] against [11 11 9]).; Repeat receipt e0ef28c2bc89481aa6b3af478422de7c reproduced all three modes of the original probe with the same values: with RestoreCommittedLogs and no snapshot the node returns with an empty configuration and does not lead again (index 1), while the non-replay mode keeps its configuration and leads (index 3) and the snapshot mode keeps its configuration and leads (index 5).; Repeat receipt 2963a0b01d97404dbf946e7b87a214f8 reproduced the partial-restart outcome exactly (two restarted voters with empty configurations, the untouched voter leading at index 2 with nodes_with_full=1, then no leader among the two live voters holding log index 13 apiece; control re-electing at index 0), so the live-quorum progress loss is reproducible as well.; The revised dual-majority execution (receipt 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903) scored all three comparisons as predicted: the committed entry is truncated after healing (violated, witness 7), the FSMs diverge after an acknowledged write (violated, witness 7, fsm_a_logs 6 against fsm_b_logs 5), and the stale leader confirmed leadership while the old majority led in a higher term (violated, witness 6: verify_ok true, old_leader B in term 4, a_still_leader true).; The repeat of the client-contract revision (receipt 108a83830e904d90a9236738033c2c74) reproduced all three comparison outcomes (truncation violated at witness 7, FSM divergence violated at witness 7, confirmation-while-another-leader violated at witness 6 with verify_ok true, old_leader B in term 4 and A still leading), so that consequence is reproducible.; The repair execution also acts as counterevidence against reading the stale configuration as irrecoverable: a later configuration entry from a correctly configured leader restored the forgotten voter on the restarted node (receipt 6d6abaf163524e64878c6c9810de2461, comparison and witness index 5).; Boundary control: with the same operations but without the commits that push the persisted commit index past the removal entry, the restarted node keeps the committed membership and the removed voter stays removed (receipt 457abd18451d4fd18ed506ae7f5c5391, comparison and witness index 9), so the loss is tied to the entry lying inside the replayed prefix and not to the restart or the removal itself.; The boundary control repeated: receipt 4fe974e4e3cc491984791b8a812c5886 reproduced every comparison of the boundary revision (resurrection violated at index 1, premature commit violated at index 3, flag-off control holding at index 7, and the shallow case holding at index 9 with two servers and the removed voter absent), so the trigger boundary is reproducible and not a schedule artifact.; Counterevidence that limits the impact of the cluster-wide loss rather than the finding: the same stores, restarted once more with the flag disabled, came back fully configured and elected a leader (receipt 81163da076c64417bd48e0f79260d73d, comparison and witness index 2), so the state is operator-recoverable without touching durable data.; Causal refinement, observed rather than argued: the same stores and the same flag produced a good outcome while nothing had been staged and the failure once the flag-on path had staged a commit index (receipt 656e33fb90f24c58a94928eeeeb938aa, comparison holds at index 1 and violated at index 3), so the deciding condition is the persisted commit index named in the trigger, not merely enabling the feature.; Causal refinement reproduced: repeat receipt 202311f4911e4af5828d49134f37811c produced the identical values and outcomes (staged zero with the configuration kept through the first flagged restart, holds at index 1; staged nine afterwards and the configuration lost on the next one, violated at witness index 3), so the contrast that pins the trigger to the persisted commit index is stable across executions.; Record-keeping limitation, not a counterexample to any claim: the stored repair Fact lists four sources and three receipts while its corrected statement and conditions were merged; the missing receipt (6d6abaf163524e64878c6c9810de2461 index 5) and the four named source anchors are cited here and in the interpretations that rely on them, so no claim rests on the shortened list.
Interpretation limitations: All executions are in-process in-memory clusters at protocol version 3 with 50ms heartbeat/election timeouts and a single committed configuration change; joint-consensus or multi-step changes are not exercised.; The finding is specific to RestoreCommittedLogs=true with a CommitTrackingLogStore; with the flag disabled the same durable state recovers normally in every receipt.; The configuration-less nodes still act as voters in other respects (they granted the configured voter's election win in receipt 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837, index 0), which is why the cluster survived until that voter stopped; this is read from the receipt and from the membership checks being skipped for an empty configuration (raft.go 1663-1672, 1780-1784).; In that probe the partitioned side elects its leader with 3s election timeouts (reloaded to keep the restarted leader from losing the first election), so the interval is seconds; the ordering it demonstrates does not depend on those particular values.; The dual-majority probe has no control variant: with the flag disabled the leader's configuration is current, so the same AddVoter is a single-server change and cannot create disjoint majorities (nextConfiguration over the current configuration, configuration.go 224-302).; Leader concurrency on the two sides was observed with A still leading in four executions (receipts 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c, 11dea1fdcb6d4f089a373fe6c1d3a36e, 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903 and 108a83830e904d90a9236738033c2c74) while one revision of the harness observed A already stepped down when the old side's leader was sampled, so the window is real but its length is schedule-dependent; the reproducible consequences are the truncation of the committed entry and the resulting FSM divergence.; The child question is now established by retained receipt 226f9762f0b444f69c154b35fe0788f3 (resurrected membership and a write applied on the leader with B, required by the committed configuration, never receiving the entry; control refuses the same write), so the parents' consequence list includes premature commitment under a stale membership.; Two consequences reached by later receipts are no longer pending: the cluster-wide and partial-restart progress losses (receipts 4f4a771f03b649c2a5703b0ff279ff3a and 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837) and the premature-commit-under-a-stale-membership consequence (receipt 226f9762f0b444f69c154b35fe0788f3 with its repeat 7adf927d528b4a74942c03b155aa8557).; A source check of which snapshot the library considers newest found the expected protection: SnapshotStore implementations rank candidates by term then index (file_snapshot.go 535-547 with List at 286), so the newest snapshot is selected; no evidence of a snapshot-selection defect was found, and none is claimed.; The third consequence direction is now established by retained receipt b1daa1f4c9444b8d857bc7e0ab761691: a restarted leader that forgets an added voter accepted a write held by only two of the four committed voters, while the control refused it.; A check of the captured documentation found no statement about this feature outside the source: RestoreCommittedLogs and CommitTrackingLogStore appear only in config.go, log.go and api.go, and never in README.md, docs/README.md, docs/apply.md, docs/divergence.md, membership.md or CHANGELOG.md (those files do mention snapshots elsewhere, so the search itself is sound). The only normative text is the Config field comment, which requires the commit-tracking store but nothing about snapshots or configuration recovery, so no documented caller duty defeats the premise.; In the original probe and its repeat the two control modes share the comparison event names with the failing mode, so their comparisons are scored unknown; the scored control for the non-replay restart comes from the separate isolated-control experiment (receipt edfd3c204c654542a8bdb4263f290d4d, holds).; Correction of the repair-path statement: an earlier version of the summary said only a snapshot install or an operator restart repairs a stale configuration. A later configuration entry does too, because appendEntries processes new configuration entries and installs the membership encoded in them (raft.go 1569-1578); the three repair paths are now stated explicitly. This correction does not change any comparison or receipt; it narrows the persistence claim.; The client-contract consequence is now established by retained receipt 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903: VerifyLeader returned success on the stale-membership leader (its own acknowledgement plus the promoted voter's) in the same execution in which the old majority elected B in term 4 while that leader still considered itself leader, so the documented protection against returning stale data does not hold in this state.; The repair path is now executed as well: receipt 6d6abaf163524e64878c6c9810de2461 (index 5) shows the stale node restored to five members including the forgotten voter D and the newly added E once a correctly configured leader replicated a later configuration entry to it, with the other four comparisons in that execution unchanged (membership violated at index 1, premature commit violated at index 3, controls holding at indices 7 and 9). Boundary that follows: repair needs a correctly configured leader, so it is available where the stale nodes are a minority (the forgotten-voter case) and unavailable where the empty configuration prevents any leader from being elected (the cluster-wide and partial-restart cases).; Process note kept for traceability: receipt 8f0b76d0cd49441c81ecb603f1fcd527 is a build failure of the superseded revision of the partial-restart harness (helpers declared in a sibling file that is not copied for execution); my repeat request had named that superseded experiment instead of its correction b826595f01b844f9b95efe7b29d757dd-experiment. The receipt carries no evidence and is deliberately absent from this interpretation's executions map because a build failure yields no parsed observations; the cited partial-restart observations come only from the corrected revision.; The trigger boundary is now executed in both directions by receipt 457abd18451d4fd18ed506ae7f5c5391: in the shallow case the staged commit index is 5 while the removal entry sits at index 6, so the scan covers it and the restarted node keeps the committed membership (comparison holds at index 9: two servers, removed voter absent, one peer, and the partitioned write refused), whereas the same harness with two extra commits has the removal entry at index 7 with staged commit 7 and resurrects the removed voter (violated at index 1) and accepts the write (violated at index 3; control holds at index 7). The condition 'configuration entry at or below the persisted commit index' in the trigger summary is therefore execution-confirmed rather than reasoned.; Boundary of the empty-configuration case, kept explicit because it limits the consequence: what is lost is membership context and the ability to campaign, not data flow. In the partial-restart receipts (7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837 and its repeat 2963a0b01d97404dbf946e7b87a214f8) the two configuration-less nodes still appended and applied entries up to log index 13 while the correctly configured voter led, and they still granted the votes that let it win, so replication through a configured leader continues; the observable harm is their empty self-view (no campaigns, no peers) and, once the configured voter stops, the cluster-wide loss of electability recorded in those same receipts.; Citation audit: every receipt index cited by the current interpretations was re-read from the retained observations and matches the claim it supports (empty configuration and no leadership at 430d7ba602ed4666bdfe63a96c71e2fc index 1 and its repeat e0ef28c2bc89481aa6b3af478422de7c index 1; all three voters empty at 4f4a771f03b649c2a5703b0ff279ff3a index 1 and c1dcda29549b48c7a775adfc2e9a4bda index 1; no leader among the two live voters at 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837 index 1 and 2963a0b01d97404dbf946e7b87a214f8 index 1; silent change, concurrent leader and truncation at 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c indices 2, 3, 4; leader confirmation, confirmation-while-another-leader and truncation plus FSM divergence at 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903 indices 4, 6, 7 and confirmation-while-another-leader again at 108a83830e904d90a9236738033c2c74 index 6; stale membership and the dropped voter at d2d1cb0951b74a2984ec525710e4c740 indices 1 and 3; applied client write and FSM divergence at e5ad9e5149fa4255b61e7826bf6b8064 indices 3 and 5; resurrection and premature commit at 226f9762f0b444f69c154b35fe0788f3 indices 1 and 3 and their repeat 7adf927d528b4a74942c03b155aa8557 indices 1 and 3; forgotten voter and understated quorum at b1daa1f4c9444b8d857bc7e0ab761691 indices 1 and 3 and repeat ec2c61af79bd42d7a5fe00657b7aeb22 indices 1 and 3; repair at 6d6abaf163524e64878c6c9810de2461 index 5; boundary at 457abd18451d4fd18ed506ae7f5c5391 indices 1 and 9 and its repeat 4fe974e4e3cc491984791b8a812c5886 indices 1 and 9).; Reachability boundary on the snapshot repair path: although an installed snapshot does carry the configuration (raft.go 1953-1961), a leader sends a snapshot only when the follower lacks entries the leader has already compacted, and a node whose configuration was lost this way has a complete log (the loss comes from skipping entries, not from missing them), so no snapshot is sent to it in these scenarios (with the caveat, found while re-reading the snapshot path, that a leader-side user restore leaves a hole above such a node's next index and does send it one, replication.go 222-224 with raft.go 1097-1199). The snapshot path therefore repairs new or behind nodes, while a stale-but-complete node is repaired only by an operator restart without the flag or by a later configuration entry from a correctly configured leader, as executed.; Operator recovery is now executed (receipt 0440f054115e44f4a0234c7a4ef67150): in the empty-configuration state live bootstrap refuses with 'bootstrap only works on new clusters' and leaves the node empty (violated, index 1), while RecoverCluster on the stopped node restores the supplied configuration and the node leads again within three seconds (holds, index 2). The repair picture is therefore complete and operational: a later configuration entry from a correctly configured leader, a restart with the flag disabled, or RecoverCluster on a stopped node; not live bootstrap, and not an incoming snapshot for a node whose log is already complete.; The operator remediation for the cluster-wide case is now executed (receipt 81163da076c64417bd48e0f79260d73d): the flagged simultaneous restart left every voter empty with no leader (violated, index 1, staged commit indices [11 11 11]), and stopping the same three nodes and restarting them on the same stores with the flag disabled restored the configuration on all three and produced a leader (holds at index 2, nodes_with_full_config 3, leader index 1; control unchanged at index 4). The consequence of the headline progress loss is therefore bounded: it is in-memory and reversible by an ordinary restart, with no durable state discarded and no configuration change needed, but nothing in-protocol can repair it while it lasts.; Precision on what the truncation removes, taken from the same receipts rather than reasoned: in both executions that carry the client write (e5ad9e5149fa4255b61e7826bf6b8064 index 5 and 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903 index 7) the stale leader's log end falls from index 12 to 11 after healing while its applied index stays at 12 and its FSM still holds six commands against the new leader's five. The entry removed is therefore not only the configuration change at index 11 but also the client command the leader had committed and applied at index 12, and the two sides' applied state differs by exactly that command. This is the client-visible form of the safety violation: an acknowledged write is deleted from the log of the node that acknowledged it, while the divergent FSM keeps its effect.; The causal refinement is executed (receipt 656e33fb90f24c58a94928eeeeb938aa): the cluster that had only run with the flag disabled carried a staged commit index of 0 and kept its configuration through the first flagged restart (comparison holds, index 1), then staged 9 through its own writes while the flag was on (index 2) and lost the configuration on the next flagged restart (violated, witness index 3, zero servers and no leader). The trigger is therefore the persisted commit index relative to the newest configuration entry, not the flag by itself, and the first restart after enabling the feature can look harmless.; The latent-trap experiment has been executed twice with identical values (receipts 656e33fb90f24c58a94928eeeeb938aa and 202311f4911e4af5828d49134f37811c), so the causal refinement rests on a reproduced contrast rather than a single run.; Traceability note on one knowledge record, so a reviewer is not misled by its evidence list: two submissions that supplied the repair Fact's sources and executions were accepted but not reflected in the stored entry (revisions 4 and 5 keep four source ids and three receipts). Its statement and conditions are the corrected ones, and the evidence exists in the rest of the record: the in-protocol repair by a later configuration entry is receipt 6d6abaf163524e64878c6c9810de2461 index 5, cited in the parent and in the forgotten-voter interpretation and executed with its own comparisons; the operator paths are receipt 0440f054115e44f4a0234c7a4ef67150 (live bootstrap refusing at index 1, RecoverCluster repairing at index 2) and 81163da076c64417bd48e0f79260d73d (flag-disabled restart restoring all voters at index 2), both cited here; and the source anchors that the entry's list omits are the bootstrap refusal (api.go 260-267), RecoverCluster (api.go 321-448), the snapshot trigger (replication.go 222-224) and the user-restore hole (raft.go 1097-1199), all of which are declared in this submission's sources.
