Interpretation counterevidence: The isolated control receipt edfd3c204c654542a8bdb4263f290d4d scores holds with the identical restart and no snapshot (servers_after=1), so the loss is caused by replaying the committed prefix, not by restart, snapshot absence, or the commit-tracking store.; The snapshot run inside the first receipt (index 5) keeps the configuration, so the defect requires the newest configuration entry to be inside the skipped prefix; a snapshot taken after the change masks it.; Voter C never runs in the two-voter probe, so nothing in the receipts shows C resisting or noticing its removal; the claim is about the configuration the running nodes decide with.; The cluster-wide receipt 4f4a771f03b649c2a5703b0ff279ff3a scores the control comparison holds (index 3, nodes_with_full_config=3) and the failing case violated (index 1, nodes_with_full_config=0), so the empty configuration after a simultaneous restart is specific to the replayed committed prefix.; Receipt 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837 scores the control comparison holds (index 3: the two live voters re-elect a leader without the flag) and the failing case violated (index 1: after the configured voter stops, no leader among the two live voters although both hold every committed entry, log last index 13 on both), so the loss of electability is tied to the missing configuration rather than to the restart or the shutdown.; The dual-majority path needs a caught-up nonvoter E so the silent change can commit without the partitioned voter B; without such a node the change would need B's acknowledgement and B would then hold the new membership.; Two independent executions of the corrected dual-majority experiment (receipts 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c and 11dea1fdcb6d4f089a373fe6c1d3a36e) produced the same entry index, the same concurrent leadership and the same truncation, so the outcome is reproducible rather than a single-run timing artifact.; In that extended execution the stale leader had already stepped down when the old side's leader was sampled (index 4, a_still_leader=false), which is why leader concurrency is reported as an observed window from the two earlier executions rather than as a comparison in the current harness.; Repeat receipt c1dcda29549b48c7a775adfc2e9a4bda reproduced the simultaneous-restart outcome exactly (servers_after [0,0,0], nodes_with_full_config 0, no leader in the observation window; control [3,3,3] with a leader elected at index 3), so the cluster-wide progress loss is reproducible under schedule variation (the staged commit indices differed from the first run: [11 10 11] against [11 11 9]).; Repeat receipt e0ef28c2bc89481aa6b3af478422de7c reproduced all three modes of the original probe with the same values: with RestoreCommittedLogs and no snapshot the node returns with an empty configuration and does not lead again (index 1), while the non-replay mode keeps its configuration and leads (index 3) and the snapshot mode keeps its configuration and leads (index 5).; Repeat receipt 2963a0b01d97404dbf946e7b87a214f8 reproduced the partial-restart outcome exactly (two restarted voters with empty configurations, the untouched voter leading at index 2 with nodes_with_full=1, then no leader among the two live voters holding log index 13 apiece; control re-electing at index 0), so the live-quorum progress loss is reproducible as well.; The revised dual-majority execution (receipt 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903) scored all three comparisons as predicted: the committed entry is truncated after healing (violated, witness 7), the FSMs diverge after an acknowledged write (violated, witness 7, fsm_a_logs 6 against fsm_b_logs 5), and the stale leader confirmed leadership while the old majority led in a higher term (violated, witness 6: verify_ok true, old_leader B in term 4, a_still_leader true).; The repeat of the client-contract revision (receipt 108a83830e904d90a9236738033c2c74) reproduced all three comparison outcomes (truncation violated at witness 7, FSM divergence violated at witness 7, confirmation-while-another-leader violated at witness 6 with verify_ok true, old_leader B in term 4 and A still leading), so that consequence is reproducible.; The repair execution also acts as counterevidence against reading the stale configuration as irrecoverable: a later configuration entry from a correctly configured leader restored the forgotten voter on the restarted node (receipt 6d6abaf163524e64878c6c9810de2461, comparison and witness index 5).; Boundary control: with the same operations but without the commits that push the persisted commit index past the removal entry, the restarted node keeps the committed membership and the removed voter stays removed (receipt 457abd18451d4fd18ed506ae7f5c5391, comparison and witness index 9), so the loss is tied to the entry lying inside the replayed prefix and not to the restart or the removal itself.; The boundary control repeated: receipt 4fe974e4e3cc491984791b8a812c5886 reproduced every comparison of the boundary revision (resurrection violated at index 1, premature commit violated at index 3, flag-off control holding at index 7, and the shallow case holding at index 9 with two servers and the removed voter absent), so the trigger boundary is reproducible and not a schedule artifact.; Counterevidence that limits the impact of the cluster-wide loss rather than the finding: the same stores, restarted once more with the flag disabled, came back fully configured and elected a leader (receipt 81163da076c64417bd48e0f79260d73d, comparison and witness index 2), so the state is operator-recoverable without touching durable data.; Causal refinement, observed rather than argued: the same stores and the same flag produced a good outcome while nothing had been staged and the failure once the flag-on path had staged a commit index (receipt 656e33fb90f24c58a94928eeeeb938aa, comparison holds at index 1 and violated at index 3), so the deciding condition is the persisted commit index named in the trigger, not merely enabling the feature.; Causal refinement reproduced: repeat receipt 202311f4911e4af5828d49134f37811c produced the identical values and outcomes (staged zero with the configuration kept through the first flagged restart, holds at index 1; staged nine afterwards and the configuration lost on the next one, violated at witness index 3), so the contrast that pins the trigger to the persisted commit index is stable across executions.; Record-keeping limitation, not a counterexample to any claim: the stored repair Fact lists four sources and three receipts while its corrected statement and conditions were merged; the missing receipt (6d6abaf163524e64878c6c9810de2461 index 5) and the four named source anchors are cited here and in the interpretations that rely on them, so no claim rests on the shortened list.
Interpretation limitations: All executions are in-process in-memory clusters at protocol version 3 with 50ms heartbeat/election timeouts and a single committed configuration change; joint-consensus or multi-step changes are not exercised.; The finding is specific to RestoreCommittedLogs=true with a CommitTrackingLogStore; with the flag disabled the same durable state recovers normally in every receipt.; The configuration-less nodes still act as voters in other respects (they granted the configured voter's election win in receipt 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837, index 0), which is why the cluster survived until that voter stopped; this is read from the receipt and from the membership checks being skipped for an empty configuration (raft.go 1663-1672, 1780-1784).; In that probe the partitioned side elects its leader with 3s election timeouts (reloaded to keep the restarted leader from losing the first election), so the interval is seconds; the ordering it demonstrates does not depend on those particular values.; The dual-majority probe has no control variant: with the flag disabled the leader's configuration is current, so the same AddVoter is a single-server change and cannot create disjoint majorities (nextConfiguration over the current configuration, configuration.go 224-302).; Leader concurrency on the two sides was observed with A still leading in four executions (receipts 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c, 11dea1fdcb6d4f089a373fe6c1d3a36e, 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903 and 108a83830e904d90a9236738033c2c74) while one revision of the harness observed A already stepped down when the old side's leader was sampled, so the window is real but its length is schedule-dependent; the reproducible consequences are the truncation of the committed entry and the resulting FSM divergence.; The child question is now established by retained receipt 226f9762f0b444f69c154b35fe0788f3 (resurrected membership and a write applied on the leader with B, required by the committed configuration, never receiving the entry; control refuses the same write), so the parents' consequence list includes premature commitment under a stale membership.; Two consequences reached by later receipts are no longer pending: the cluster-wide and partial-restart progress losses (receipts 4f4a771f03b649c2a5703b0ff279ff3a and 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837) and the premature-commit-under-a-stale-membership consequence (receipt 226f9762f0b444f69c154b35fe0788f3 with its repeat 7adf927d528b4a74942c03b155aa8557).; A source check of which snapshot the library considers newest found the expected protection: SnapshotStore implementations rank candidates by term then index (file_snapshot.go 535-547 with List at 286), so the newest snapshot is selected; no evidence of a snapshot-selection defect was found, and none is claimed.; The third consequence direction is now established by retained receipt b1daa1f4c9444b8d857bc7e0ab761691: a restarted leader that forgets an added voter accepted a write held by only two of the four committed voters, while the control refused it.; A check of the captured documentation found no statement about this feature outside the source: RestoreCommittedLogs and CommitTrackingLogStore appear only in config.go, log.go and api.go, and never in README.md, docs/README.md, docs/apply.md, docs/divergence.md, membership.md or CHANGELOG.md (those files do mention snapshots elsewhere, so the search itself is sound). The only normative text is the Config field comment, which requires the commit-tracking store but nothing about snapshots or configuration recovery, so no documented caller duty defeats the premise.; In the original probe and its repeat the two control modes share the comparison event names with the failing mode, so their comparisons are scored unknown; the scored control for the non-replay restart comes from the separate isolated-control experiment (receipt edfd3c204c654542a8bdb4263f290d4d, holds).; Correction of the repair-path statement: an earlier version of the summary said only a snapshot install or an operator restart repairs a stale configuration. A later configuration entry does too, because appendEntries processes new configuration entries and installs the membership encoded in them (raft.go 1569-1578); the three repair paths are now stated explicitly. This correction does not change any comparison or receipt; it narrows the persistence claim.; The client-contract consequence is now established by retained receipt 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903: VerifyLeader returned success on the stale-membership leader (its own acknowledgement plus the promoted voter's) in the same execution in which the old majority elected B in term 4 while that leader still considered itself leader, so the documented protection against returning stale data does not hold in this state.; The repair path is now executed as well: receipt 6d6abaf163524e64878c6c9810de2461 (index 5) shows the stale node restored to five members including the forgotten voter D and the newly added E once a correctly configured leader replicated a later configuration entry to it, with the other four comparisons in that execution unchanged (membership violated at index 1, premature commit violated at index 3, controls holding at indices 7 and 9). Boundary that follows: repair needs a correctly configured leader, so it is available where the stale nodes are a minority (the forgotten-voter case) and unavailable where the empty configuration prevents any leader from being elected (the cluster-wide and partial-restart cases).; Process note kept for traceability: receipt 8f0b76d0cd49441c81ecb603f1fcd527 is a build failure of the superseded revision of the partial-restart harness (helpers declared in a sibling file that is not copied for execution); my repeat request had named that superseded experiment instead of its correction b826595f01b844f9b95efe7b29d757dd-experiment. The receipt carries no evidence and is deliberately absent from this interpretation's executions map because a build failure yields no parsed observations; the cited partial-restart observations come only from the corrected revision.; The trigger boundary is now executed in both directions by receipt 457abd18451d4fd18ed506ae7f5c5391: in the shallow case the staged commit index is 5 while the removal entry sits at index 6, so the scan covers it and the restarted node keeps the committed membership (comparison holds at index 9: two servers, removed voter absent, one peer, and the partitioned write refused), whereas the same harness with two extra commits has the removal entry at index 7 with staged commit 7 and resurrects the removed voter (violated at index 1) and accepts the write (violated at index 3; control holds at index 7). The condition 'configuration entry at or below the persisted commit index' in the trigger summary is therefore execution-confirmed rather than reasoned.; Boundary of the empty-configuration case, kept explicit because it limits the consequence: what is lost is membership context and the ability to campaign, not data flow. In the partial-restart receipts (7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837 and its repeat 2963a0b01d97404dbf946e7b87a214f8) the two configuration-less nodes still appended and applied entries up to log index 13 while the correctly configured voter led, and they still granted the votes that let it win, so replication through a configured leader continues; the observable harm is their empty self-view (no campaigns, no peers) and, once the configured voter stops, the cluster-wide loss of electability recorded in those same receipts.; Citation audit: every receipt index cited by the current interpretations was re-read from the retained observations and matches the claim it supports (empty configuration and no leadership at 430d7ba602ed4666bdfe63a96c71e2fc index 1 and its repeat e0ef28c2bc89481aa6b3af478422de7c index 1; all three voters empty at 4f4a771f03b649c2a5703b0ff279ff3a index 1 and c1dcda29549b48c7a775adfc2e9a4bda index 1; no leader among the two live voters at 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837 index 1 and 2963a0b01d97404dbf946e7b87a214f8 index 1; silent change, concurrent leader and truncation at 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c indices 2, 3, 4; leader confirmation, confirmation-while-another-leader and truncation plus FSM divergence at 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903 indices 4, 6, 7 and confirmation-while-another-leader again at 108a83830e904d90a9236738033c2c74 index 6; stale membership and the dropped voter at d2d1cb0951b74a2984ec525710e4c740 indices 1 and 3; applied client write and FSM divergence at e5ad9e5149fa4255b61e7826bf6b8064 indices 3 and 5; resurrection and premature commit at 226f9762f0b444f69c154b35fe0788f3 indices 1 and 3 and their repeat 7adf927d528b4a74942c03b155aa8557 indices 1 and 3; forgotten voter and understated quorum at b1daa1f4c9444b8d857bc7e0ab761691 indices 1 and 3 and repeat ec2c61af79bd42d7a5fe00657b7aeb22 indices 1 and 3; repair at 6d6abaf163524e64878c6c9810de2461 index 5; boundary at 457abd18451d4fd18ed506ae7f5c5391 indices 1 and 9 and its repeat 4fe974e4e3cc491984791b8a812c5886 indices 1 and 9).; Reachability boundary on the snapshot repair path: although an installed snapshot does carry the configuration (raft.go 1953-1961), a leader sends a snapshot only when the follower lacks entries the leader has already compacted, and a node whose configuration was lost this way has a complete log (the loss comes from skipping entries, not from missing them), so no snapshot is sent to it in these scenarios (with the caveat, found while re-reading the snapshot path, that a leader-side user restore leaves a hole above such a node's next index and does send it one, replication.go 222-224 with raft.go 1097-1199). The snapshot path therefore repairs new or behind nodes, while a stale-but-complete node is repaired only by an operator restart without the flag or by a later configuration entry from a correctly configured leader, as executed.; Operator recovery is now executed (receipt 0440f054115e44f4a0234c7a4ef67150): in the empty-configuration state live bootstrap refuses with 'bootstrap only works on new clusters' and leaves the node empty (violated, index 1), while RecoverCluster on the stopped node restores the supplied configuration and the node leads again within three seconds (holds, index 2). The repair picture is therefore complete and operational: a later configuration entry from a correctly configured leader, a restart with the flag disabled, or RecoverCluster on a stopped node; not live bootstrap, and not an incoming snapshot for a node whose log is already complete.; The operator remediation for the cluster-wide case is now executed (receipt 81163da076c64417bd48e0f79260d73d): the flagged simultaneous restart left every voter empty with no leader (violated, index 1, staged commit indices [11 11 11]), and stopping the same three nodes and restarting them on the same stores with the flag disabled restored the configuration on all three and produced a leader (holds at index 2, nodes_with_full_config 3, leader index 1; control unchanged at index 4). The consequence of the headline progress loss is therefore bounded: it is in-memory and reversible by an ordinary restart, with no durable state discarded and no configuration change needed, but nothing in-protocol can repair it while it lasts.; Precision on what the truncation removes, taken from the same receipts rather than reasoned: in both executions that carry the client write (e5ad9e5149fa4255b61e7826bf6b8064 index 5 and 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903 index 7) the stale leader's log end falls from index 12 to 11 after healing while its applied index stays at 12 and its FSM still holds six commands against the new leader's five. The entry removed is therefore not only the configuration change at index 11 but also the client command the leader had committed and applied at index 12, and the two sides' applied state differs by exactly that command. This is the client-visible form of the safety violation: an acknowledged write is deleted from the log of the node that acknowledged it, while the divergent FSM keeps its effect.; The causal refinement is executed (receipt 656e33fb90f24c58a94928eeeeb938aa): the cluster that had only run with the flag disabled carried a staged commit index of 0 and kept its configuration through the first flagged restart (comparison holds, index 1), then staged 9 through its own writes while the flag was on (index 2) and lost the configuration on the next flagged restart (violated, witness index 3, zero servers and no leader). The trigger is therefore the persisted commit index relative to the newest configuration entry, not the flag by itself, and the first restart after enabling the feature can look harmless.; The latent-trap experiment has been executed twice with identical values (receipts 656e33fb90f24c58a94928eeeeb938aa and 202311f4911e4af5828d49134f37811c), so the causal refinement rests on a reproduced contrast rather than a single run.; Traceability note on one knowledge record, so a reviewer is not misled by its evidence list: two submissions that supplied the repair Fact's sources and executions were accepted but not reflected in the stored entry (revisions 4 and 5 keep four source ids and three receipts). Its statement and conditions are the corrected ones, and the evidence exists in the rest of the record: the in-protocol repair by a later configuration entry is receipt 6d6abaf163524e64878c6c9810de2461 index 5, cited in the parent and in the forgotten-voter interpretation and executed with its own comparisons; the operator paths are receipt 0440f054115e44f4a0234c7a4ef67150 (live bootstrap refusing at index 1, RecoverCluster repairing at index 2) and 81163da076c64417bd48e0f79260d73d (flag-disabled restart restoring all voters at index 2), both cited here; and the source anchors that the entry's list omits are the bootstrap refusal (api.go 260-267), RecoverCluster (api.go 321-448), the snapshot trigger (replication.go 222-224) and the user-restore hole (raft.go 1097-1199), all of which are declared in this submission's sources.; Artifact check: the ten harness files in this draft were hashed against the controller's fixed copies, and each current experiment's harness matches the draft byte for byte (primary probe 9c549c026d7341f2b1e328826eac6dc3, gap probe 8efd0d1e3da9484e926cab983024d9c3, partial-restart correction b826595f01b844f9b95efe7b29d757dd, cluster-wide remediation d2938865782c439380ed920dd69f8d7a, dual-majority verify revision cae69864c3a4406ba6f2c5d594bda44c, resurrect boundary revision dd13767ee8154cd3b8253d6352f679da, understate repair revision 6856b3402bb5458ba40e94f9f7e3ea00, operator recovery 82a49b6bfe414dbab6903379c966b105, isolated control d2cb2558b564427ba5f166e377991a07, latent trap eb30543c698b432c8f570dbfc31951f6). The fixed copies that do not match a current draft file are the superseded revisions of those same lineages (81237e6441414088bfb2079263cc63ec, a8b8d696ac934beda1434a93b5d7758f, cdee42fcadd7460991a44622a9725658, 981f67969ef44bc1b4d8e296cbb610c4, cff2222705354f669ca24cef6629804a, f79f8f8c97204c7d9c76b1a2b8ca07a0, d5ed22414b9d439e9d0fcd0b06849027, dd5cdfe7274a4444b305c5d104f6e5c8), which is the expected state: their receipts remain valid for the comparisons they scored, and the current bytes are the corrected revisions.; Detection, from the fields this investigation already read rather than from a new API: GetConfiguration and Stats report the node's in-memory configuration and its index (api.go 1231-1237 and the GetConfiguration accessor), so the state is found by comparing that configuration with the configuration a peer reports or with the newest configuration entry in the node's own store, not by a threshold on indexes. The two forms observed here are an empty in-memory configuration (the empty case, seen as zero servers and zero peers while the node still holds a complete log) and an in-memory configuration older than the newest configuration entry in that node's log (the stale case, e.g. two servers while peers report three or four). One caution against a false positive: latest_configuration_index being below commit_index is normal, because a configuration entry stays the latest until a later configuration entry appears while ordinary entries continue to commit, so that comparison alone does not indicate this state.; Protection direction, following directly from the traced mechanism rather than from any new claim: the state exists because the configuration scan begins after the replayed committed prefix (api.go 611-613), so scanning configuration entries from the snapshot index onward instead of from max(lastSnapshot, lastApplied)+1 would leave the replayed entries applied to the FSM while still rebuilding the configuration from the log; and because the failure is silent, a start-time check that compares the reconstructed configuration with the newest configuration entry the node's own log or snapshot carries (and refuses to serve, or reports, when a voter's configuration is empty or older than that entry) would surface the state where indexes alone cannot, since the log is complete and commit and applied indexes look healthy.; Source-anchor audit of this submission's own grounding, run in the closing pass and reported because it is checkable rather than new evidence: all 24 declared sources were re-read from the captured tree and each one still lands on the code or text it is cited for, including the load-bearing anchors of the finding (the configuration scan and its max(lastSnapshot, lastApplied)+1 bound at api.go 601-622, restoreFromCommittedLogs raising lastApplied to the commit-tracking store's index at api.go 723-755, the snapshot-configuration restore at api.go 645-689 and processConfigurationLogEntry at raft.go 1605-1623) and the anchors of the consequences and boundaries (raft.go 1663-1672 and 1780-1784 for the skipped membership checks, raft.go 1204-1241 and 1236-1241 for configuration-change admission and commit-on-append, configuration.go 224-302 for nextConfiguration, raft.go 964-988 for the verifyLeader quorum, raft.go 1953-1961 and 1569-1578 for the two repair-by-installation paths, api.go 260-267 and api.go 321-448 for the bootstrap refusal and RecoverCluster, replication.go 222-224 with raft.go 1097-1199 for the snapshot trigger and the user-restore hole). No anchor was found to be off by a line or attached to a different construct, so no correction followed from the audit; it is recorded here because the whole account rests on these ranges having been read in the captured tree rather than in an editor.
Gap responses: 9c549c026d7341f2b1e328826eac6dc3-gap-0: model declares resolved: Resolved by retained receipt d2d1cb0951b74a2984ec525710e4c740: the restarted node adopts the snapshot-carried configuration when the newest configuration entry lies inside the replayed committed prefix (comparison 0 violated, witness index 1: servers_after=2 while the peer reports 3 and the newest configuration entry index 8 is below the staged commit index 11), and that stale base changes a real decision (comparison 2 violated, witness index 3: AddVoter E returned no error and both nodes ended with 3 members and contains_c_final=false, so voter C was silently removed). The same receipt's control mode kept 3 members and ended with 4 including C (observed at parsed index 5; that comparison was scored unknown because both modes shared a result event name, which the dedicated control experiment has now replaced with a scored holds).; a8b8d696ac934beda1434a93b5d7758f-gap-1: model declares resolved: Resolved affirmatively by retained receipts 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c, 11dea1fdcb6d4f089a373fe6c1d3a36e, 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903 and 108a83830e904d90a9236738033c2c74: the silently created two-server change {A,B,C} -> {A,B,E} commits on the stale leader A plus the promoted, caught-up nonvoter E while the old voter B is partitioned (witness index 2 in each execution: change_err nil, committed true, the configuration entry present on A and on E, B still one index short); the old majority {B,C} then elects B in a higher term while A still leads its own configuration with E's acknowledgements (witness index 3 or 6: old_leader B in term 4 with a_still_leader true); and after the partition heals A's committed entry is replaced by the new leader's entry (witness index 7, committed_entry_truncated true), leaving the two sides with different logs and different applied state (fsm_a_logs 6 against fsm_b_logs 5). The direct route the earlier answer identified as impossible stays impossible - a voter that never receives the entry is strictly behind and is refused by voters that hold it (raft.go 1731-1746, 1812-1828) - which is exactly why the construction needs the entry to commit without one old voter, made possible by the promoted nonvoter and by the new configuration entering the commitment on append (raft.go 1236-1241).; 1ed9540f22fe4fa9bef3b3bda88e22e8-gap-2: model declares resolved: Resolved by retained receipt 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c (scored): the silent two-server change {A,B,C} -> {A,B,E} committed on A plus the promoted caught-up nonvoter E (parsed index 2: change_err nil, x_index 11, committed=true, entry type LogConfiguration on A and on E, A commit index 11, B still at log index 10); the old majority {B,C} elected B in term 4 while A was still leader in term 3 (parsed index 3, comparison violated with witness 3), i.e. two concurrent leaders with disjoint support over the same log; and after healing, A's entry at index 11 became a LogNoop of term 4 (parsed index 4, comparison violated with witness 4), so the entry committed under the configuration recorded in the logs was truncated on the node that had committed it. The earlier receipt 79d93a5aaad448888cc04214be8f2ad8 reproduced the same observations but its comparisons were unscored because of my identity wiring; it is retained as the superseded revision of the same harness.
### When RestoreCommittedLogs makes a restarted leader forget a committed removal, does the resurrected voter let that leader commit and report success for entries that the configuration committed in the log requires another member (B) to accept?

Current disposition: active.

Interpretation limitations: The partition is an explicit transport disconnection between A and B; the removed voter C is up and caught up, which is required for A to see a quorum in its stale view.; The repeat execution reproduced the same values and outcomes under the same setup (entry index 10, A commit and applied 10, B at 9, control refusing the write), so the premature-commit observation is not a single-run artifact.; The shallow boundary and the failing path have now been executed twice each with identical values (receipts 457abd18451d4fd18ed506ae7f5c5391 and 4fe974e4e3cc491984791b8a812c5886).
Parent question: `9c549c026d7341f2b1e328826eac6dc3-question-0`; this result does not automatically close its parent.
Hypothesis: Yes: A's in-memory configuration still contains the removed voter C, so A's commitment quorum is computed over {A,B,C} and an entry acknowledged by A and C counts as committed even though the configuration committed in the log is {A,B}; A applies it and the client is told it succeeded although B, a member required for any quorum of the committed configuration, never received the entry.
Registered discriminator: Same cluster and stores with the flag on and off: shut down C, remove it, commit further entries, restart the leader, bring C back so it catches up, partition B, then apply one entry on the leader. Prediction with the flag: the Apply returns success, the leader's commit and applied indexes advance to the new entry, and the entry is absent from B (and from every quorum of {A,B}). Prediction without the flag: the leader's configuration is {A,B}, so the same partition makes the same Apply fail.

Fixed experiment `981f67969ef44bc1b4d8e296cbb610c4-experiment` v1: [saved basis](fixed-experiments/981f67969ef44bc1b4d8e296cbb610c4-experiment/basis.json).
Scope: Three-voter in-process cluster {A,B,C} at protocol version 3 with 50ms timeouts. A snapshots, then C is shut down for its own removal, RemoveServer C commits with {A,B}, two further commands push the persisted commit index past the removal entry, and A is restarted on the same stores with RestoreCommittedLogs (case restore_on) or without it (control restore_off). The restarted A's configuration and peer count are observed against B's. Then C is brought back on its old stores so it catches up from A, B is partitioned from A, and one Apply is issued on A; the probe records whether the Apply succeeded, the entry index, A's commit and applied indexes, whether the entry reached B, and the FSM lengths on both sides.
History / supplied conditions: Real bootstrap of all three voters, real snapshot, real RemoveServer, real commits, real shutdown/restart of the leader and of the removed voter on the same InmemCommitTrackingStore/InmemStore/InmemSnapshotStore instances, real transport reconnection and real partition. No fabricated configuration or log state.
Assumptions: C is offline for its own removal, so it never learns it was removed; that is an ordinary operator sequence (a failed node is removed while down and then comes back).; B and C both hold every entry up to the removal, so the entries, commit index and configurations come from real replication.; After the partition, {A,B} is the configuration committed in the log (removal entry committed), so an entry present only on A cannot be committed.
Excluded scope: No disk faults or message loss; the only partition is the explicit disconnection of B.; The probe does not assert what happens after the partition heals, which is the subject of the dual-majority harness.
Declared requirement / prediction: No fixed requirement; observations remain available for sourced interpretation.

### When RestoreCommittedLogs makes a restarted leader forget a voter whose addition is committed in its own log, does the resulting smaller in-memory quorum let it accept and apply entries that only a minority of the committed voters hold?

Current disposition: active.
Question `d5ed22414b9d439e9d0fcd0b06849027-question-2` v1; sources: newraft_scan, restore_committed, snapshot_config, append_config_entry, next_configuration, commit_config_on_append ([full references](state.json)).
Current model defect claim: defect asserted (subject to independent verification).

Current interpretation `0312653e48e0448bb8c613b8f01e66f7-interpretation-2` · declared predicate does not hold: Retained receipt b1daa1f4c9444b8d857bc7e0ab761691 scores all four comparisons as predicted. After a committed AddVoter D and a restart with RestoreCommittedLogs, the leader reports three servers and no longer contains D while the other three nodes report four (comparison 0 violated, witness index 1). With C and D disconnected, a single Apply on that leader succeeds: it commits and applies the entry at index 8 while C's log ends at 7 and D's at 6, so only two of the four committed voters hold it and the entry is not committed under the configuration in the log, which requires three (comparison 2 violated, witness index 3, voters_holding_entry=2, entry_on_committed_quorum=false). The controls hold: the same restart without the flag keeps four servers (index 5) and the same partition makes the write fail with 'leadership lost while committing log' (index 7). Mechanism: the in-memory configuration drives the quorum (configurationChangeChIfStable admits changes on stale indexes, appendConfigurationEntry derives membership from the stale base, commitment is installed from it on append), so a configuration missing a committed voter understates the quorum and lets the client be told a write succeeded.

Parent question: `9c549c026d7341f2b1e328826eac6dc3-question-0`; this result does not automatically close its parent.
Hypothesis: Yes: with the added voter D absent from the restarted leader's configuration, its quorum is two of {A,B,C} instead of three of {A,B,C,D}, so a partition that leaves only A and B connected still lets it commit and apply an entry, and the client is told the write succeeded although a quorum of the committed configuration never received it.
Registered discriminator: Four voters {A,B,C}+D added after a snapshot, further commits, then restart the leader with the flag on and off; partition C and D from A and apply one entry. Prediction with the flag: the Apply succeeds and only A and B hold the entry; prediction without the flag: the same partition makes the Apply fail.

Fixed experiment `d5ed22414b9d439e9d0fcd0b06849027-experiment` v1: [saved basis](fixed-experiments/d5ed22414b9d439e9d0fcd0b06849027-experiment/basis.json).
Scope: Four in-process nodes at protocol version 3 with 50ms timeouts. A is bootstrapped with voters {A,B,C}, all four run, A snapshots, commits a command, adds D as a voter (committed configuration {A,B,C,D}, quorum three) and commits two further commands. A is restarted on the same stores with RestoreCommittedLogs (case restore_on) or without it (control restore_off), with the other three nodes' timeouts lengthened so the restarted leader wins its re-election. The probe records the restarted leader's configuration against the others, then partitions C and D from A and applies one entry, recording whether the Apply succeeded, the entry index, A's commit and applied indexes, each voter's log tail, and how many of the four committed voters hold the entry.
History / supplied conditions: Real bootstrap, real snapshot, real AddVoter with catch-up, real commits, real shutdown and restart of the leader on the same InmemCommitTrackingStore/InmemStore/InmemSnapshotStore instances, real transport partition. Nothing is fabricated.
Assumptions: D is caught up before the restart, so the committed configuration genuinely has four voters (quorum three).; C and D are disconnected in both directions, which is a real partition for all Raft traffic; A and B remain connected.; The committed configuration {A,B,C,D} requires three acknowledgements, so an entry held by A and B only is not committed under it.
Excluded scope: No disk faults or message loss; the only partition is the explicit disconnection of C and D.; D is kept on the normal restart path (flag disabled) so its own configuration recovery cannot confound the observation.
Declared requirement / prediction: No fixed requirement; observations remain available for sourced interpretation.

Historical interpretation `c0d9b4afce654f6e95af0049a6dae161-interpretation-2` · declared predicate does not hold; model defect claim: defect asserted (subject to independent verification): Retained receipt b1daa1f4c9444b8d857bc7e0ab761691 scores all four comparisons as predicted. After a committed AddVoter D and a restart with RestoreCommittedLogs, the leader reports three servers and no longer contains D while the other three nodes report four (comparison 0 violated, witness index 1). With C and D disconnected, a single Apply on that leader succeeds: it commits and applies the entry at index 8 while C's log ends at 7 and D's at 6, so only two of the four committed voters hold it and the entry is not committed under the configuration in the log, which requires three (comparison 2 violated, witness index 3, voters_holding_entry=2, entry_on_committed_quorum=false). The controls hold: the same restart without the flag keeps four servers (index 5) and the same partition makes the write fail with 'leadership lost while committing log' (index 7). Mechanism: the in-memory configuration drives the quorum (configurationChangeChIfStable admits changes on stale indexes, appendConfigurationEntry derives membership from the stale base, commitment is installed from it on append), so a configuration missing a committed voter understates the quorum and lets the client be told a write succeeded.

Sources: [newraft_scan](state.json), [restore_committed](state.json), [snapshot_config](state.json), [append_config_entry](state.json), [next_configuration](state.json), [commit_config_on_append](state.json); execution evidence: [b1daa1f4c9444b8d857bc7e0ab761691](logs/b1daa1f4c9444b8d857bc7e0ab761691/check.json) ([observations](logs/b1daa1f4c9444b8d857bc7e0ab761691/observations.json), event indices [1, 3]).
Interpretation counterevidence: The control mode on identical stores and the identical partition refuses the write, so the acceptance is attributable to the understated membership rather than to the partition.
Interpretation limitations: The probe partitions C and D explicitly; a construction-time repeat is requested in this update because the outcome depends on the restarted leader winning its re-election and on the partition leaving A and B connected.; The example uses four voters; the size of the understatement grows with the number of voters added after the snapshot, so this probe understates rather than overstates the margin.

## Other research results

### When a node's in-memory configuration is empty after a restart with RestoreCommittedLogs, what can an operator actually do: does live bootstrap on the running node repair it, and does the documented RecoverCluster path on the stopped node repair it?

Current disposition: active.
Question `82a49b6bfe414dbab6903379c966b105-question-3` v1; sources: newraft_scan, restore_committed, cfg_doc ([full references](state.json)).
Current model defect claim: no explicit defect claim submitted.

Current interpretation `0312653e48e0448bb8c613b8f01e66f7-interpretation-3` · source explanation: Retained receipt 0440f054115e44f4a0234c7a4ef67150 answers what an operator can do in the state this investigation identified. The state itself reproduced (parsed index 0: zero servers, no leader within two seconds, staged commit 6, log last index 7). Live bootstrap on the running node failed with 'bootstrap only works on new clusters' and left the configuration empty (parsed index 1, comparison violated): that is the documented refusal, since BootstrapCluster checks HasExistingState and returns ErrCantBootstrap when a term, log or snapshot exists (api.go 260-267), which is exactly this state. RecoverCluster on the stopped node succeeded and the following NewRaft came up with one server and led within three seconds (parsed index 2, comparison holds): it restores any snapshot, replays the log into the supplied FSM, writes a new snapshot carrying the supplied configuration and truncates the log (api.go 321-448), so the next NewRaft takes its configuration from that snapshot instead of from the replayed prefix that the defect skips. The library therefore does provide a repair path for a stopped node, but not for a running one and not in-protocol; no defect is claimed about either behaviour, and the value of the observation is operational: it distinguishes a path that works from one that does not in the state the defect creates.

Sources: [newraft_scan](state.json), [restore_committed](state.json), [cfg_doc](state.json), [bootstrap_refusal](state.json), [recover_cluster](state.json), [snapshot_config](state.json); execution evidence: [0440f054115e44f4a0234c7a4ef67150](logs/0440f054115e44f4a0234c7a4ef67150/check.json) ([observations](logs/0440f054115e44f4a0234c7a4ef67150/observations.json), event indices [1, 2]).
Interpretation counterevidence: The two outcomes point in opposite directions and both match the documented contracts, so neither is evidence against the finding: the repair that works requires stopping the node and supplying the configuration explicitly, while the running node cannot repair itself.
Interpretation limitations: Single-voter cluster; RecoverCluster's success is shown on a node whose stores are otherwise intact, which is the state the defect leaves behind (complete log, missing in-memory configuration).; RecoverCluster is documented as an unsafe, explicit disaster-recovery operation; its success here is a repair capability, not a normal operating path.
Parent question: `9c549c026d7341f2b1e328826eac6dc3-question-0`; this result does not automatically close its parent.
Hypothesis: Live bootstrap does not help, because it refuses when the cluster is not new (existing term, log and snapshots), while RecoverCluster does repair the node: it reads the existing state, writes a snapshot carrying the supplied configuration and truncates the log, so the next NewRaft restores that configuration from the snapshot instead of from the skipped log prefix.
Registered discriminator: Single-voter cluster bootstrapped, commands committed, node restarted with the flag so its configuration is empty; then (a) call BootstrapCluster on the running node and record the error and the configuration size, and (b) stop the node, run RecoverCluster with the same stores and the original configuration, start it again and record the configuration size and whether it leads.

### Does a node restarted with RestoreCommittedLogs=true, whose newest configuration entry is inside the persisted commit index and has no covering snapshot, still know that configuration after NewRaft returns?

Current disposition: active.
Question `4099b8f3cc5c45d2b3c3049ce5a5c0de-question-0` v1; sources: newraft_scan, restore_committed, newraft_doc, cfg_doc, snapshot_config, process_config_entry, follower_abort, commit_index_staging ([full references](state.json)).
Current model defect claim: no explicit defect claim submitted.
Hypothesis: No. restoreFromCommittedLogs sets lastApplied to the persisted commit index, so the configuration scan starts after the committed prefix and never calls processConfigurationLogEntry for the configuration entry that only exists in the log. r.configurations.latest stays empty (or stays at the snapshot configuration), so the node loses its own membership context, cannot start elections, and skips the membership checks when granting votes.
Registered discriminator: Restart the same durable state twice: with RestoreCommittedLogs=true and with RestoreCommittedLogs=false. Predict servers_after=0 and no re-election with the feature on, versus servers_after=1 and a successful re-election with it off. A third run takes a snapshot before restart to show that a snapshot-carried configuration masks the loss (servers_after=1), separating the scanning bound from generic restart damage.

## Shared understanding and revisions

- `dd5cdfe7274a4444b305c5d104f6e5c8-knowledge-0` r2 · fact: NewRaft does not restore a configuration entry that lies inside the replayed committed log prefix: with RestoreCommittedLogs enabled the configuration comes only from the newest snapshot plus configuration entries above max(lastSnapshot, persistedCommitIndex), so a node restarted from a log whose newest configuration entry is at or below the persisted commit index adopts the snapshot configuration (empty when there is no snapshot) instead of the replicated one.; conditions: RestoreCommittedLogs=true; LogStore implements CommitTrackingLogStore; node started on stores whose persisted commit index is at or above the newest configuration entry index; no snapshot whose ConfigurationIndex covers that entry..

- `1a8ca5d0b10a4e248b1d2d93c8656a9e-knowledge-1` r3 · behavior: A stale in-memory configuration drives every membership decision of the node: configurationChangeChIfStable admits a configuration change once the stale latest and committed indexes look equal, appendConfigurationEntry derives the next membership from the stale base, commitment is installed from that new configuration on append, and the election quorum, checkLeaderLease and the leadership-confirmation quorum (verifyLeader) all use the latest in-memory configuration. After a restart with RestoreCommittedLogs a node can therefore drop a voter that is only in its log, resurrect a voter whose removal is committed, and count a quorum of the stale membership: it commits and applies entries that a member required by the committed configuration has not accepted, it confirms leadership for clients from that stale quorum while a different majority elects a leader in a higher term, and with a partitioned old voter it can truncate an entry it had committed.; conditions: RestoreCommittedLogs=true with a CommitTrackingLogStore and a log whose newest configuration entry lies inside the replayed committed prefix without a covering snapshot; the affected node must lead (or be elected) for the commitment, lease, confirmation and configuration-change consequences..

- `6420ecc11ae840028bf3e70220f5fd17-knowledge-1` r5 · fact: A configuration that a node holds only in its log can be restored to that node's in-memory state by four paths, of which only one is in-protocol: a later configuration entry replicated by a correctly configured leader (appendEntries processes new configuration entries); an operator restart with RestoreCommittedLogs disabled; RecoverCluster on the stopped node with the configuration supplied, which writes a snapshot carrying it and truncates the log so the next NewRaft restores it from the snapshot; and an installed snapshot, whose metadata carries the configuration. In the restart scenarios recorded here none of the four is triggered by the node's own restart: a leader sends a snapshot only to a follower that lacks already-compacted entries (replication.go 222-224), and the affected node's log is complete, so no snapshot is sent to it and no configuration entry reaches it uncommitted. The snapshot path is nevertheless reachable for a node with a complete log whenever the leader's own log has a hole above that node's next index, as after a leader-side user restore, which deliberately leaves such a hole (raft.go 1097-1199). Where every voter restarts with the flag enabled and no covering snapshot, the in-protocol path needs a leader that the empty configuration prevents from being elected, so the cluster stays unavailable until an operator acts.; conditions: RestoreCommittedLogs=true with a CommitTrackingLogStore and configuration entries inside the replayed committed prefix. Observed with: a four-voter cluster in which a stale node is a minority (in-protocol repair by a later configuration entry, and the no-repair case); three voters all restarted at once (no in-protocol repair and no leader); and a single-voter cluster in the empty-configuration state for the operator paths (live bootstrap refusing, RecoverCluster succeeding, and the flag-disabled restart restoring all voters)..
  Prior r1: A configuration that a node only holds in its log can be restored to that node's in-memory state by exactly three paths, and only two of them are in-protocol: a later configuration entry replicated by a correctly configured leader (appendEntries processes new configuration entries), an installed snapshot (whose metadata carries the configuration), or a restart with RestoreCommittedLogs disabled. Where every voter restarts with RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and no covering snapshot, the first two paths need a leader, which the empty configuration prevents from being elected, so the cluster stays unavailable until an operator acts.; correction: Statement corrected and extended: the previous revision enumerated exactly three repair paths and did not mention RecoverCluster. The operator-recovery execution (receipt 0440f054115e44f4a0234c7a4ef67150) established a fourth path — RecoverCluster on a stopped node with the configuration supplied — and a path that explicitly does not work, live bootstrap on the running node, which refuses with ErrCantBootstrap while leaving the configuration empty, as well as the earlier reachability boundary that no snapshot is sent to a node whose log is complete. The conditions and source list are extended accordingly; earlier executions and the claims they support are unchanged.; affected uses: none registered.
